entries.bc18487db0eb918cd5363b5a3482038148ea09e2: <div sID="gen4797" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="8" osisID="Judg.8" sID="Judg.8"/> <div eID="gen4797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4798" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen4799" type="x-p"/> This chapter gives us a further account of Gideon's victory over the Midianites, with the residue of the story of his life and government. I. Gideon prudently pacifies the offended Ephraimites, <reference osisRef="Judg.8.1-Judg.8.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. He bravely pursues the flying Midianites, <reference osisRef="Judg.8.4">ver. 4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Judg.8.10-Judg.8.12">10-12</reference>. III. He justly chastises the insolence of the men of Succoth and Penuel, who basely abused him (<reference osisRef="Judg.8.5-Judg.8.9">ver. 5-9</reference>), and were reckoned with for it, <reference osisRef="Judg.8.13-Judg.8.17">ver. 13-17</reference>. IV. He honourably slays the two kings of Midian, <reference osisRef="Judg.8.18-Judg.8.21">ver. 18-21</reference>. V. After all this he modestly declines the government of Israel, <reference osisRef="Judg.8.22-Judg.8.23">ver. 22, 23</reference>. VI. He foolishly gratified the superstitious humour of his people by setting up an ephod in his own city, which proved a great snare, <reference osisRef="Judg.8.24-Judg.8.27">ver. 24-27</reference>. VII. He kept the country quiet for forty years, <reference osisRef="Judg.8.28">ver. 28</reference>. VIII. He died in honour, and left a numerous family behind him, <reference osisRef="Judg.8.29-Judg.8.32">ver. 29-32</reference>. IX. Both he and his God were soon forgotten by ungrateful Israel, <reference osisRef="Judg.8.33-Judg.8.35">ver. 33-35</reference>.
entries.2c22d989862a3d50d23e7d3764ee1a9fb1d2839a: <div eID="gen4799" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen4798" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Gideon Pacifies the Ephraimites. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1249.)</title> <div sID="gen4800" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And the men of Ephraim said unto him, Why hast thou served us thus, that thou calledst us not, when thou wentest to fight with the Midianites? And they did chide with him sharply. <hi type="super">2</hi> And he said unto them, What have I done now in comparison of you? <hi type="italic">Is</hi> not the gleaning of the grapes of Ephraim better than the vintage of Abiezer? <hi type="super">3</hi> God hath delivered into your hands the princes of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb: and what was I able to do in comparison of you? Then their anger was abated toward him, when he had said that. <div eID="gen4800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4801" type="x-p"/> No sooner were the Midianites, the common enemy, subdued, than, through the violence of some hot spirits, the children of Israel were ready to quarrel among themselves; an unhappy spark was struck, which, if Gideon had not with a great deal of wisdom and grace extinguished immediately, might have broken out into a flame of fatal consequence. The Ephraimites, when they brought the heads of Oreb and Zeeb to Gideon as general, instead of congratulating him upon his successes and addressing him with thanks for his great services, as they ought to have done, picked a quarrel with him and grew very hot upon it. <div eID="gen4801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4802" type="x-p"/> I. Their accusation was very peevish and unreasonable: <hi type="italic">Why didst thou not call us when thou wentest to fight with the Midianites?</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.7.1">v. 1</reference>. Ephraim was brother to Manasseh, Gideon's tribe, and had the pre-eminence in Jacob's blessing and in Moses's, and therefore was very jealous of Manasseh, lest that tribe should at any time eclipse the honour of theirs. Hence we find Manasseh against Ephraim and Ephraim against Manasseh, <reference osisRef="Isa.9.21">Isa. ix. 21</reference>. <hi type="italic">A brother offended is harder to be won than a strong city, and their contentions are as the bars of a castle,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.18.19">Prov. xviii. 19</reference>. But how unjust was their quarrel with Gideon! They were angry that he did not send for them to begin the attack upon Midian, as well as to follow the blow. Why were they not called to lead the van? The post of honour, they thought, belonged to them. But, 1. Gideon was called of God, and must act as he directed; he neither took the honour to himself nor did he himself dispose of honours, but left it to God to do all. So that the Ephraimites, in this quarrel, reflected upon the divine conduct; and what was Gideon that they <hi type="italic">murmured against him?</hi> 2. Why did not the Ephraimites offer themselves willingly to the service? They knew the enemy was in their country, and had heard of the forces that were raising to oppose them, to which they ought to have joined themselves, in zeal for the common cause, though they had not a formal invitation. Those seek themselves more than God that stand upon a point of honour to excuse themselves from doing real service to God and their generation. In Deborah's time there was a root of Ephraim, <reference osisRef="Judg.5.14">ch. v. 14</reference>. Why did not this appear now? The case itself called them, they needed not wait for a call from Gideon. 3. Gideon had saved their credit in not calling them. If he had sent for them, no doubt may of them would have gone back with the faint-hearted, or been dismissed with the lazy, slothful, and intemperate; so that by not calling them he prevented the putting of those slurs upon them. Cowards will seem valiant when the danger is over, but those consult their reputation who try not their courage when danger is near. <div eID="gen4802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4803" type="x-p"/> II. Gideon's answer was very calm and peaceable, and was intended not so much to justify himself as to please and pacify them, <reference osisRef="Judg.7.2-Judg.7.3">v. 2, 3</reference>. He answers them, 1. With a great deal of meekness and temper. He did not resent the affront, nor answer anger with anger, but mildly reasoned the case with them, and he won as true honour by this command which he had over his own passion as by his victory over the Midianites. <hi type="italic">He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty.</hi> 2. With a great deal of modesty and humility, magnifying their performances above his own: <hi type="italic">Is not the gleaning of the grapes of Ephraim,</hi> who picked up the stragglers of the enemy, and cut off those of them that escaped, <hi type="italic">better than the vintage of Abiezer</hi>—a greater honour to them, and better service to the country, than the first attack Gideon made upon them? The destruction of the church's enemies is compared to a vintage, <reference osisRef="Rev.14.18">Rev. xiv. 18</reference>. In this he owns their gleanings better than his gatherings. The improving of a victory is often more honourable, and of greater consequence, than the winning of it; in this they had signalized themselves, and their own courage and conduct, or, rather, God had dignified them; for thought, to magnify their achievements, he is willing to diminish his own performances, yet he will not take any flowers from God's crown to adorn theirs with: "<hi type="italic">God has delivered into your hands the princes of Midian,</hi> and a great slaughter has been made of the enemy by your numerous hosts, and <hi type="italic">what was I able to do</hi> with 300 men, <hi type="italic">in comparison of you</hi> and your brave exploits?" Gideon stands here a very great example of self-denial, and this instance shows us, (1.) That humility of deportment is the best way to remove envy. It is true even right works are often envied, <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.4">Eccl. iv. 4</reference>. Yet they are not so apt to be so when those who do them appear not to be proud of them. Those are malignant indeed who seek to cast down from their excellency those that humble and abase themselves, (2.) It is likewise the surest method of ending strife, for <hi type="italic">only by pride comes contention,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.13.10">Prov. xiii. 10</reference>. (3.) Humility is most amiable and admirable in the midst of great attainments and advancements. Gideon's conquests did greatly set off his condescensions. (4.) It is the proper act of humility to <hi type="italic">esteem others better than ourselves,</hi> and <hi type="italic">in honour to prefer one another.</hi> <div eID="gen4803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4804" type="x-p"/> Now what was the issue of this controversy? The Ephraimites had <hi type="italic">chidden with him sharply</hi> (<reference osisRef="Judg.7.1">v. 1</reference>), forgetting the respect due to their general and one whom God had honoured, and giving vent to their passion in a very indecent liberty of speech, a certain sign of a weak and indefensible cause. Reason runs low when the chiding flies high. But Gideon's <hi type="italic">soft answer turned away their wrath,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.15.1">Prov. xv. 1</reference>. <hi type="italic">Their anger was abated towards him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.7.3">v. 3</reference>. It is intimated that they retained some resentment, but he prudently overlooked it and let it cool by degrees. Very great and good men must expect to have their patience tried by the unkindnesses and follies even of those they serve and must not think it strange.
entries.8f308cdfea58a035916e2c2ede2aff95ec322e1b: <div eID="gen4804" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Gideon Pursues the Midianites. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1249.)</title> <div sID="gen4805" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> And Gideon came to Jordan, <hi type="italic">and</hi> passed over, he, and the three hundred men that <hi type="italic">were</hi> with him, faint, yet pursuing <hi type="italic">them.</hi> <hi type="super">5</hi> And he said unto the men of Succoth, Give, I pray you, loaves of bread unto the people that follow me; for they <hi type="italic">be</hi> faint, and I am pursuing after Zebah and Zalmunna, kings of Midian. <hi type="super">6</hi> And the princes of Succoth said, <hi type="italic">Are</hi> the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna now in thine hand, that we should give bread unto thine army? <hi type="super">7</hi> And Gideon said, Therefore when the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath delivered Zebah and Zalmunna into mine hand, then I will tear your flesh with the thorns of the wilderness and with briers. <hi type="super">8</hi> And he went up thence to Penuel, and spake unto them likewise: and the men of Penuel answered him as the men of Succoth had answered <hi type="italic">him.</hi> <hi type="super">9</hi> And he spake also unto the men of Penuel, saying, When I come again in peace, I will break down this tower. <hi type="super">10</hi> Now Zebah and Zalmunna <hi type="italic">were</hi> in Karkor, and their hosts with them, about fifteen thousand <hi type="italic">men,</hi> all that were left of all the hosts of the children of the east: for there fell an hundred and twenty thousand men that drew sword. <hi type="super">11</hi> And Gideon went up by the way of them that dwelt in tents on the east of Nobah and Jogbehah, and smote the host: for the host was secure. <hi type="super">12</hi> And when Zebah and Zalmunna fled, he pursued after them, and took the two kings of Midian, Zebah and Zalmunna, and discomfited all the host. <hi type="super">13</hi> And Gideon the son of Joash returned from battle before the sun <hi type="italic">was up,</hi> <hi type="super">14</hi> And caught a young man of the men of Succoth, and enquired of him: and he described unto him the princes of Succoth, and the elders thereof, <hi type="italic">even</hi> threescore and seventeen men. <hi type="super">15</hi> And he came unto the men of Succoth, and said, Behold Zebah and Zalmunna, with whom ye did upbraid me, saying, <hi type="italic">Are</hi> the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna now in thine hand, that we should give bread unto thy men <hi type="italic">that are</hi> weary? <hi type="super">16</hi> And he took the elders of the city, and thorns of the wilderness and briers, and with them he taught the men of Succoth. <hi type="super">17</hi> And he beat down the tower of Penuel, and slew the men of the city. <div eID="gen4805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4806" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have, <div eID="gen4806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4807" type="x-p"/> I. Gideon, as a valiant general, pursuing the remaining Midianites, and bravely following his blow. A very great slaughter was made of the enemy at first: 120,000 <hi type="italic">men that drew the sword,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.7.10">v. 10</reference>. Such a terrible execution did they make among themselves, and so easy a prey were they to Israel. But, it seems, the two kings of Midian, being better provided than the rest for an escape, with 15,000 men got over Jordan before the passes could be secured by the Ephraimites, and made towards their own country. Gideon thinks he does not fully execute his commission to save Israel if he let them escape. He is not content to chase them out of the country, but he will <hi type="italic">chase them out of the world,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.18.18">Job xviii. 18</reference>. This resolution is here pushed on with great firmness, and crowned with great success. <div eID="gen4807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4808" type="x-p"/> 1. His firmness was very exemplary. He effected his purpose under the greatest disadvantages and discouragements that could be. (1.) He took none with him but his 300 men, who now laid aside their trumpets and torches, and betook themselves to their swords and spears. God had said, <hi type="italic">By these 300 men will I save you</hi> (<reference osisRef="Judg.7.7">ch. vii. 7</reference>); and, confiding in that promise, Gideon kept to them only, <reference osisRef="Judg.7.4">v. 4</reference>. He expected more from 300 men, supported by a particular promise, than from so many thousands supported only by their own valour. (2.) They were <hi type="italic">faint, and yet pursuing,</hi> much fatigued with what they had done, and yet eager to do more against the enemies of their country. Our spiritual warfare must thus be prosecuted with what strength we have, though we have but little; it is many a time the true Christina's case, fainting and yet pursuing. (3.) Though he met with discouragement from those of his own people, was jeered for what he was doing, as going about what he could never accomplish, yet he went on with it. If those that should be our helpers in the way of our duty prove hindrances to us, let not this drive us off from it. Those know not how to value God's acceptance that know not how to despise the reproaches and contempts of men. (4.) He made a very long march by <hi type="italic">the way of those that dwelt in tents</hi> (<reference osisRef="Judg.7.11">v. 11</reference>), either because he hoped to find them kinder to him than the men of Succoth and Penuel, that dwelt in walled towns (sometimes there is more generosity and charity found in country tents than in city palaces), or because that was a road in which he would be least expected, and therefore that way it would be the greater surprise to them. It is evident he spared no pains to complete his victory. Now he found it an advantage to have his 300 men such as could bear hunger, and thirst, and toil. It should seem, he set upon the enemy by night, as he had done before, for <hi type="italic">the host was secure.</hi> The security of sinners often proves their ruin, and dangers are most fatal when least feared. <div eID="gen4808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4809" type="x-p"/> 2. His success was very encouraging to resolution and industry in a good cause. He routed the army (<reference osisRef="Judg.7.11">v. 11</reference>), and took the two kings prisoners, <reference osisRef="Judg.7.12">v. 12</reference>. Note, The fear of the wicked shall come upon him. Those that think to run <hi type="italic">from the sword of the Lord and of Gideon</hi> do but run <hi type="italic">upon</hi> it. If he <hi type="italic">flee from the iron weapon,</hi> yet <hi type="italic">the bow of steel shall strike him through;</hi> for <hi type="italic">evil pursueth sinners.</hi> <div eID="gen4809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4810" type="x-p"/> II. Here is Gideon, as a righteous judge, chastising the insolence of the disaffected Israelites, the men of Succoth and the men of Penuel, both in the tribe of Gad, on the other side Jordan. <div eID="gen4810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4811" type="x-p"/> 1. Their crime was great. Gideon, with a handful of feeble folk was pursuing the common enemy, to complete the deliverance of Israel. His way led him through the city of Succoth first and afterwards of Penuel. He expected not that the magistrates should meet him in their formalities, congratulate him upon his victory, present him with the keys of their city, and give him a treat, much less that they should send forces in to his assistance, though he was entitled to all this; but he only begs some necessary food for his soldiers that were ready to faint for want, and he does it very humbly and importunately: <hi type="italic">Give, I pray you, loaves of bread unto the people that follow me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.7.5">v. 5</reference>. The request would have been reasonable if they had been but poor travellers in distress; but considering that they were soldiers, <hi type="italic">called, and chose, and faithful</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.17.14">Rev. xvii. 14</reference>), men whom God had greatly honoured and to whom Israel was highly obliged, who had done great service to their country and were now doing more,—that they were conquerors, and had power to put them under contribution,—and that they were fighting God's battles and Israel's,—nothing could be more just than that their brethren should furnish them with the best provisions their city afforded. But the princes of Succoth neither <hi type="italic">feared God nor regarded man.</hi> For, (1.) In contempt of God, they refused to answer the just demands of him whom God had raised up to save them, affronted him, bantered him, despised the success he had already been honoured with, despaired of the success of his present undertaking, did what they could to discourage him in prosecuting the war, and were very willing to believe that the remaining forces of Midian, which they had now seen march through their country, would be too hard for him: <hi type="italic">Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna now in thy hand?</hi> "No, nor ever will be," so they conclude, judging by the disproportion of numbers. (2.) The bowels of their compassion were shut up against their brethren; they were as destitute of love as they were of faith, would not give morsels of bread (so some read it) to those that were ready to perish. Were these princes? were these Israelites? unworthy either title, base and degenerate men! Surely they were worshippers of Baal, or in the interests of Midian. The men of Penuel gave the same answer to the same request, defying <hi type="italic">the sword of the Lord and of Gideon,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.7.8">v. 8</reference>. <div eID="gen4811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4812" type="x-p"/> 2. The warning he gave them of the punishment of their crime was very fair. (1.) He did not punish it immediately, because he would not lose so much time from the pursuit of the enemy that were flying from him, because he would not seem to do it in a neat of passion, and because he would do it more to their shame and confusion when he had completed his undertaking, which they thought impracticable. But, (2.) He told them how he would punish it (<reference osisRef="Judg.7.7">v. 7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Judg.7.9">9</reference>), to show the confidence he had of success in the strength of God, and that, if they had the least grain of grace and consideration left, they might upon second thoughts repent of their folly, humble themselves, and contrive how to atone for it, by sending after him succours and supplies, which if they had done, no doubt, Gideon would have pardoned them. God gives notice of danger, and space to repent, that sinners may <hi type="italic">flee from the wrath to come.</hi> <div eID="gen4812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4813" type="x-p"/> 3. The warning being slighted, the punishment, though very severe, was really very just. <div eID="gen4813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4814" type="x-p"/> (1.) The princes of Succoth were first made examples. Gideon got intelligence of their number, seventy-seven men, their names, and places of abode, which were described in writing to him, <reference osisRef="Judg.7.14">v. 14</reference>. And, to their great surprise, when they thought he had scarcely overtaken the Midianites, he returned a conqueror. His 300 men were now the ministers of his justice; they secured all these princes, and brought them before Gideon, who showed them his royal captives in chains. "These are the men you thought me an unequal match for, and would give me no assistance in the pursuit of," <reference osisRef="Judg.7.15">v. 15</reference>. And he punished them with thorns and briers, but, it should seem, not unto death. With these, [1.] He tormented their bodies, either by scourging or by rolling them in the thorns and briers; some way or other he <hi type="italic">tore their flesh,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.7.7">v. 7</reference>. Those shall have judgment without mercy that have shown no mercy. Perhaps he observed them to be soft and delicate men, who despised him and his company for their roughness and hardiness, and therefore Gideon thus mortified them for their effeminacy. [2.] He instructed their minds: With these <hi type="italic">he taught the men of Succoth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.7.16">v. 16</reference>. The correction he gave them was intended, not for destruction, but wholesome discipline, to make them wiser and better for the future. <hi type="italic">He made them know</hi> (so the word is), made them know themselves and their folly, God and their duty, made them know who Gideon was, since they would not know by the success wherewith God had crowned him. Note, Many are taught with the briers and thorns of affliction that would not learn otherwise. God gives <hi type="italic">wisdom</hi> by <hi type="italic">the rod and reproof, chastens</hi> and <hi type="italic">teaches,</hi> and by correction <hi type="italic">opens the ear to discipline.</hi> Our blessed Saviour, though he was a Son, yet <hi type="italic">learnt obedience by the things which he suffered,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.5.8">Heb. v. 8</reference>. Let every <hi type="italic">pricking brier,</hi> and <hi type="italic">grieving thorn,</hi> especially when it becomes a <hi type="italic">thorn in the flesh,</hi> be thus interpreted, thus improved. "By this God designs to teach me; what good lesson shall I learn?" <div eID="gen4814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4815" type="x-p"/> (2.) The doom of the men of Penuel comes next, and it should seem he used them more severely than the other, for good reason, no doubt, <reference osisRef="Judg.7.17">v. 17</reference>. [1.] He <hi type="italic">beat down their tower,</hi> of which they gloried, in which they trusted, perhaps scornfully advising Gideon and his men rather to secure themselves in that than to pursue the Midianites. What men make their pride is justly by its ruin made their shame. [2.] He <hi type="italic">slew the men of the city,</hi> not all, perhaps not the elders or princes, but those that had affronted him, and those only. He slew some of the men of the city that were most insolent and abusive, for terror to the rest, and <hi type="italic">so he taught the men of Penuel.</hi>
entries.da1c0c433b062fd72e88b5b9f2f2e2df4a955799: <div eID="gen4815" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Zebah and Zalmunna Slain. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1249.)</title> <div sID="gen4816" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> Then said he unto Zebah and Zalmunna, What manner of men <hi type="italic">were they</hi> whom ye slew at Tabor? And they answered, As thou <hi type="italic">art,</hi> so <hi type="italic">were</hi> they; each one resembled the children of a king. <hi type="super">19</hi> And he said, They <hi type="italic">were</hi> my brethren, <hi type="italic">even</hi> the sons of my mother: <hi type="italic">as</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> liveth, if ye had saved them alive, I would not slay you. <hi type="super">20</hi> And he said unto Jether his firstborn, Up, <hi type="italic">and</hi> slay them. But the youth drew not his sword: for he feared, because he <hi type="italic">was</hi> yet a youth. <hi type="super">21</hi> Then Zebah and Zalmunna said, Rise thou, and fall upon us: for as the man <hi type="italic">is, so is</hi> his strength. And Gideon arose, and slew Zebah and Zalmunna, and took away the ornaments that <hi type="italic">were</hi> on their camels' necks. <div eID="gen4816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4817" type="x-p"/> Judgment began <hi type="italic">at the house of God,</hi> in the just correction of the men of Succoth and Penuel, who were Israelites, but it did not end there. The kings of Midian, when they had served to demonstrate Gideon's victories, and grace his triumphs, must now be reckoned with. 1. They are indicted for the murder of Gideon's brethren some time ago at Mount Tabor. When the children of Israel, for fear of the Midianites, made themselves <hi type="italic">dens in the mountains</hi> (<reference osisRef="Judg.6.2">ch. vi. 2</reference>), those young men, it is likely, took shelter in that mountain, where they were found by these two kings, and most basely and barbarously slain in cold blood. When he asks them <hi type="italic">what manner of men they were</hi> (<reference osisRef="Judg.7.18">v. 18</reference>), it is not because he was uncertain of the thing, or wanted proof of it; he was not so little concerned for his brethren's blood as not to enquire it out before now, nor were these proud tyrants solicitous to conceal it. But he puts that question to them that by their acknowledgment of the more than ordinary comeliness of the persons they slew their crime might appear the more heinous, and consequently their punishment the more righteous. They could not but own that, though they were found in a mean and abject condition, yet they had an unusual greatness and majesty in their countenances, not unlike Gideon himself at this time: they <hi type="italic">resembled the children of a king,</hi> born for something great. 2. Being found guilty of this murder by their own confession, Gideon, though he might have put them to death as Israel's judge for the injuries done to that people in general, as Oreb and Zeeb (<reference osisRef="Judg.7.25">ch. vii. 25</reference>), yet chooses rather to put on the character of an <hi type="italic">avenger of blood,</hi> as next of kin to the persons slain: <hi type="italic">They were my brethren,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.7.19">v. 19</reference>. Their other crimes might have been forgiven, at least Gideon would not have slain them himself, let them have answered it to the people; but <hi type="italic">the voice of his brethren's blood cries,</hi> cries <hi type="italic">to him,</hi> now it is in the power of his hand to avenge it, and therefore there is no remedy—by him must <hi type="italic">their blood be shed,</hi> though they were kings. Little did they think to hear of this so long after; but murder seldom goes unpunished even in this life. 3. The execution is done by Gideon himself with his own hand, because he was the <hi type="italic">avenger of blood;</hi> he bade his son slay them, for he was a near relation to the persons murdered, and fittest to be his father's substitute and representative, and he would thus train him up to the acts of justice and boldness, <reference osisRef="Judg.7.20">v. 20</reference>. But, (1.) The young man himself desired to be excused; he feared, though they were bound and could make no resistance, <hi type="italic">because he was yet a youth,</hi> and not used to such work: courage does not always run in the blood. (2.) The prisoners themselves desired that Gideon would excuse it (<reference osisRef="Judg.7.21">v. 21</reference>), begged that, if they must die, they might die <hi type="italic">by his own hand,</hi> which would be somewhat more honourable to them, and more easy; for by his great strength they would sooner be dispatched and rid out of their pain. <hi type="italic">As is the man, so is his strength.</hi> Either they mean it of themselves (they were men of such strength as called for a better hand than that young man's to overpower quickly) or of Gideon, "Thou art at thy full strength; he has not yet come to it; therefore be thou the executioner." From those that are grown up to maturity, it is expected that what they do in any service be done with so much the more strength. Gideon dispatched them quickly, and seized the <hi type="italic">ornaments that were on their camels' necks, ornaments like the moon,</hi> so it is in the margin, either badges of their royalty or perhaps of their idolatry, for Ashteroth was represented by the moon, as Baal by the sun. With there he took all their other ornaments, as appears <reference osisRef="Judg.7.26">v. 26</reference>, where we find that he did not put them to so good a use as one would have wished. The destruction of these two kings, and that of the two princes (<reference osisRef="Judg.7.25">ch. vii. 25</reference>) is long afterwards pleaded as a precedent in prayer for the ruin of others of the church's enemies, <reference osisRef="Ps.83.11">Ps. lxxxiii. 11</reference>, <hi type="italic">Make their nobles like Oreb and Zeeb, and all their princes as Zebah and Zalmunna,</hi> let them all be but off in like manner.
entries.f97aeccecfcc3b81c70bc3f8836f2773aa5aec7e: <div eID="gen4817" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Gideon Declines the Proffered Crown. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1249.)</title> <div sID="gen4818" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> Then the men of Israel said unto Gideon, Rule thou over us, both thou, and thy son, and thy son's son also: for thou hast delivered us from the hand of Midian. <hi type="super">23</hi> And Gideon said unto them, I will not rule over you, neither shall my son rule over you: the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall rule over you. <hi type="super">24</hi> And Gideon said unto them, I would desire a request of you, that ye would give me every man the earrings of his prey. (For they had golden earrings, because they <hi type="italic">were</hi> Ishmaelites.) <hi type="super">25</hi> And they answered, We will willingly give <hi type="italic">them.</hi> And they spread a garment, and did cast therein every man the earrings of his prey. <hi type="super">26</hi> And the weight of the golden earrings that he requested was a thousand and seven hundred <hi type="italic">shekels</hi> of gold; beside ornaments, and collars, and purple raiment that <hi type="italic">was</hi> on the kings of Midian, and beside the chains that <hi type="italic">were</hi> about their camels' necks. <hi type="super">27</hi> And Gideon made an ephod thereof, and put it in his city, <hi type="italic">even</hi> in Ophrah: and all Israel went thither a whoring after it: which thing became a snare unto Gideon, and to his house. <hi type="super">28</hi> Thus was Midian subdued before the children of Israel, so that they lifted up their heads no more. And the country was in quietness forty years in the days of Gideon. <div eID="gen4818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4819" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. Gideon's laudable modesty, after his great victory, in refusing the government which the people offered him. 1. It was honest in them to offer it: <hi type="italic">Rule thou over us, for thou hast delivered us,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.7.22">v. 22</reference>. They thought it very reasonable that he who had gone through the toils and perils of their deliverance should enjoy the honour and power of commanding them ever afterwards, and very desirable that he who in this great and critical juncture had had such manifest tokens of God's presence with him should ever afterwards preside in their affairs. Let us apply it to the Lord Jesus: he hath delivered us out of the hands of our enemies, our spiritual enemies, the worst and most dangerous, and therefore it is fit he should rule over us; for how can we be better ruled than by one that appears to have so great an interest in heaven and so great a kindness for this earth? We are delivered that we may <hi type="italic">serve him without fear,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.1.74-Luke.1.75">Luke i. 74, 75</reference>. 2. It was honourable in him to refuse it: <hi type="italic">I will not rule over you,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.7.23">v. 23</reference>. What he did was with a design to serve them, not to rule them—to make them safe, easy, and happy, not to make himself great or honourable. And, as he was not ambitious of grandeur himself, so he did not covet to entail it upon his family: "<hi type="italic">My son shall not rule over you,</hi> either while I live or when I am gone, <hi type="italic">but the Lord shall</hi> still <hi type="italic">rule over you,</hi> and constitute your judges by the special designation of his own Spirit, as he has done." This intimates, (1.) His modesty, and the mean opinion he had of himself and his own merits. He thought the honour of doing good was recompence enough for all his services, which needed not to be rewarded with the honour of bearing sway. <hi type="italic">He that is greatest, let him be your minister.</hi> (2.) His piety, and the great opinion he had of God's government. Perhaps he discerned in the people a dislike of the theocracy, or divine government, a desire of a king like the nations, and thought they availed themselves of his merits as a colourable pretence to move for this change of government. But Gideon would by no means admit it. No good man can be pleased with any honour done to himself which ought to be peculiar to God. <hi type="italic">Were you baptized in the name of Paul?</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.13">1 Cor. i. 13</reference>. <div eID="gen4819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4820" type="x-p"/> II. Gideon's irregular zeal to perpetuate the remembrance of this victory by an ephod made of the choicest of the spoils. 1. He asked the men of Israel to give him the ear-rings of their prey; for such ornaments they stripped the slain of in abundance. These he demanded, either because they were the finest gold, and therefore fittest for a religious use, or because they had had as ear-rings some superstitious signification, which he thought too well of. Aaron called for the ear-rings to make the golden calf of, <reference osisRef="Exod.32.2">Exod. xxxii. 2</reference>. These Gideon begged <reference osisRef="Judg.7.24">v. 24</reference>. And he had reason enough to think that those who offered him a crown, when he declined it, would not deny him their ear-rings, when he begged them, nor did they, <reference osisRef="Judg.7.25">v. 25</reference>. 2. He himself added the spoil he took from the kings of Midian, which, it should seem, had fallen to his share, <reference osisRef="Judg.7.26">v. 26</reference>. The generals had that part of the prey which was most splendid, the <hi type="italic">prey of divers colours,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.5.30">ch. v. 30</reference>. 3. Of this he made an ephod, <reference osisRef="Judg.7.27">v. 27</reference>. It was plausible enough, and might be well intended to preserve a memorial of so divine a victory in the judge's own city. But it was a very unadvised thing to make that memorial to be an ephod, a sacred garment. I would gladly put the best construction that can be upon the actions of good men, and such a one we are sure Gideon was. But we have reason to suspect that this ephod had, as usual, a teraphim annexed to it (<reference osisRef="Hos.3.4">Hos. iii. 4</reference>), and that, having an altar already built by divine appointment (<reference osisRef="Judg.6.26">ch. vi. 26</reference>), which he erroneously imagined he might still use for sacrifice, he intended this for an oracle, to be consulted in doubtful cases. So the learned Dr. Spencer supposes. Each tribe having now very much its government within itself, they were too apt to covet their religion among themselves. We read very little of Shiloh, and the ark there, in all the story of the Judges. Sometimes by divine dispensation, and much oftener by the transgression of men, that law which obliged them to worship only at that one altar seems not to have been so religiously observed as one would have expected, any more than afterwards, when in the reigns even of very good kings <hi type="italic">the high places were not taken away,</hi> from which we may infer that that law had a further reach as a type of Christ, by whose mediation alone all our services are accepted. Gideon therefore, through ignorance or inconsideration, sinned in making this ephod, though he had a good intention in it. Shiloh, it is true, was not far off, but it was in Ephraim, and that tribe had lately disobliged him (<reference osisRef="Judg.7.1">v. 1</reference>), which made him perhaps not care to go so often among them as his occasions would lead him to consult the oracle, and therefore he would have one nearer home. However this might be honestly intended, and at first did little hurt, yet in process of time, (1.) <hi type="italic">Israel went a whoring after it,</hi> that is, they deserted God's altar and priesthood, being fond of change, and prone to idolatry, and having some excuse for paying respect to this ephod, because so good a man as Gideon had set it up, and by degrees their respect to it grew more and more superstitious. Note, Many are led into false ways by one false step of a good man. The beginning of sin, particularly of idolatry and will-worship, <hi type="italic">is as the letting forth of water,</hi> so it has been found in the fatal corruptions of the church of Rome; therefore <hi type="italic">leave it off before it be meddled with.</hi> (2.) It became a snare to Gideon himself, abating his zeal for the house of God in his old age, and much more to his house, who were drawn by it into sin, and it proved the ruin of the family. <div eID="gen4820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4821" type="x-p"/> III. Gideon's happy agency for the repose of Israel, <reference osisRef="Judg.7.28">v. 28</reference>. The Midianites that had been so vexatious gave them no more disturbance. Gideon, though he would not assume the honour and power of a king, governed as a judge, and did all the good offices he could for his people; so that <hi type="italic">the country was in quietness forty years.</hi> Hitherto the times of Israel had been reckoned by forties. Othniel judged forty years, Ehud eighty—just two forties, Barak forty, and now Gideon forty, providence so ordering it to bring in mind the forty years of their wandering in the wilderness. <hi type="italic">Forty years long was I grieved with this generation.</hi> And see <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.6">Ezek. iv. 6</reference>. After these, Eli ruled forty years (<reference osisRef="1Sam.4.18">1 Sam. iv. 18</reference>), Samuel and Saul forty (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.21">Acts xiii. 21</reference>), David forty, and Solomon forty. Forty years is about an age.
entries.e89c5d72e8899e390e536c7a68df91fc20fd9482: <div eID="gen4821" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Israel's Return to Idolatry. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1249.)</title> <div sID="gen4822" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">29</hi> And Jerubbaal the son of Joash went and dwelt in his own house. <hi type="super">30</hi> And Gideon had threescore and ten sons of his body begotten: for he had many wives. <hi type="super">31</hi> And his concubine that <hi type="italic">was</hi> in Shechem, she also bare him a son, whose name he called Abimelech. <hi type="super">32</hi> And Gideon the son of Joash died in a good old age, and was buried in the sepulchre of Joash his father, in Ophrah of the Abiezrites. <hi type="super">33</hi> And it came to pass, as soon as Gideon was dead, that the children of Israel turned again, and went a whoring after Baalim, and made Baal-berith their god. <hi type="super">34</hi> And the children of Israel remembered not the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> their God, who had delivered them out of the hands of all their enemies on every side: <hi type="super">35</hi> Neither showed they kindness to the house of Jerubbaal, <hi type="italic">namely,</hi> Gideon, according to all the goodness which he had showed unto Israel. <div eID="gen4822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4823" type="x-p"/> We have here the conclusion of the story of Gideon. 1. He lived privately, <reference osisRef="Judg.7.29">v. 29</reference>. He was not puffed up with his great honours, did not covet a palace or castle to dwell in, but retired to the house he had lived in before his elevation. Thus that brave Roman who was called from the plough upon a sudden occasion to command the army when the action was over returned to his plough again. 2. His family was multiplied. He had many wives (therein he transgressed the law); by them he had seventy sons (<reference osisRef="Judg.7.30">v. 30</reference>), but by a concubine he had one whom he named <hi type="italic">Abimelech</hi> (which signifies, <hi type="italic">my father a king</hi>), that proved the ruin of his family, <reference osisRef="Judg.7.31">v. 31</reference>. 3. He died in honour, in a good old age, when he had lived as long as he was capable of serving God and his country; and who would desire to live any longer? And he was <hi type="italic">buried in the sepulchre of his fathers.</hi> 4. After his death the people corrupted themselves, and went all to naught. As soon as ever Gideon was dead, who had kept them close to the worship of the God of Israel, they found themselves under no restraint, and then they <hi type="italic">went a whoring after Baalim,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.7.33">v. 33</reference>. They went a whoring first after another ephod (<reference osisRef="Judg.7.27">v. 27</reference>), for which irregularity Gideon had himself given them too much occasion, and now they went a whoring after another god. False worships made way for false deities. They now chose a new god (<reference osisRef="Judg.5.8">ch. v. 8</reference>), a god of a new name, <hi type="italic">Baal-berith</hi> (a goddess, say some); Berith, some think, was Berytus, the place where the Phoenicians worshipped this idol. The name signifies <hi type="italic">the Lord of a covenant.</hi> Perhaps he was so called because his worshippers joined themselves by covenant to him, in imitation of Israel's covenanting with God; for the devil is God's ape. In this revolt of Israel to idolatry they showed, (1.) Great ingratitude to God (<reference osisRef="Judg.7.34">v. 34</reference>): <hi type="italic">They remembered not the Lord,</hi> not only who had delivered them into the hands of their enemies, to punish them for their idolatry, but who had also <hi type="italic">delivered them out of the hands of their enemies,</hi> to invite them back again into his service; both the judgments and the mercies were forgotten, and the impressions of them lost. (2.) Great ingratitude to Gideon, <reference osisRef="Judg.7.35">v. 35</reference>. A great deal of <hi type="italic">goodness he had shown unto Israel,</hi> as a father to his country, for which they ought to have been kind to his family when he was gone, for that is one way by which we ought to show ourselves grateful to our friends and benefactors, and may be returning their kindnesses when they are in their graves. But Israel showed not this kindness to Gideon's family, as we shall find in the next chapter. No wonder if those who forget their God forget their friends.  <chapter eID="Judg.8"/> <div eID="gen4823" type="x-p"/>

entries.08097bc903c4f7f0e7d9e9b82644bcbeda0311e7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2295"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 8</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Judg.8.1-Judg.8.9">Jud 8:1-9</reference>. The Ephraimites Offended, but Pacified.</title> <div sID="gen3095" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2295"/><hi type="bold">1. the men of Ephraim said unto him, Why hast thou served us thus?--</hi>Where this complaint was made, whether before or after the crossing of the Jordan, cannot be determined. By the overthrow of the national enemy, the Ephraimites were benefited as largely as any of the other neighboring tribes. But, piqued at not having been sharers in the glory of the victory, their leading men could not repress their wounded pride; and the occasion only served to bring out an old and deep-seated feeling of jealous rivalry that subsisted between the tribes (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.21">Is 9:21</reference>). The discontent was groundless, for Gideon acted according to divine directions. Besides, as their tribe was conterminous with that of Gideon, they might, had they been really fired with the flame of patriotic zeal, have volunteered their services in a movement against the common enemy. <div eID="gen3095" type="x-p"/>
entries.3b30a44fafe56b33b79ea8352e2ac378e3a97d63: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2296"/><div sID="gen3096" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2296"/><hi type="bold">2-3. he said unto them, What have I done now in comparison of you?--</hi>His mild and truly modest answer breathes the spirit of a great as well as good man, who was calm, collected, and self-possessed in the midst of most exciting scenes. It succeeded in throwing oil on the troubled waters (<reference osisRef="Prov.16.1">Pr 16:1</reference>), and no wonder, for in the height of generous self-denial, it ascribes to his querulous brethren a greater share of merit and glory than belonged to himself (<reference osisRef="1Cor.13.4">1Co 13:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.2.3">Php 2:3</reference>). <div eID="gen3096" type="x-p"/>
entries.ab6857dc010d77cf1fa244fcf26d3da269591534: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2297"/><div sID="gen3097" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2297"/><hi type="bold">4. Gideon came to Jordan, and passed over--</hi>much exhausted, but eager to continue the pursuit till the victory was consummated. <div eID="gen3097" type="x-p"/>
entries.d4250f857394b162698c3b73191b37790b19d3df: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2298"/><div sID="gen3098" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2298"/><hi type="bold">5. he said unto the men of Succoth--</hi>that is, a place of tents or booths. The name seems to have been applied to the whole part of the Jordan valley on the west, as well as on the east side of the river, all belonging to the tribe of Gad (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.33.17">Ge 33:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.7.46">1Ki 7:46</reference>; with <reference osisRef="Josh.13.27">Jos 13:27</reference>). Being engaged in the common cause of all Israel, he had a right to expect support and encouragement from his countrymen everywhere. <div eID="gen3098" type="x-p"/>
entries.b7961ecb243037c92b2a14579a8648e76c4558dc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2299"/><div sID="gen3099" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2299"/><hi type="bold">6. the princes of Succoth said, Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna now in thine hand--</hi>an insolent as well as a time-serving reply. It was insolent because it implied a bitter taunt that Gideon was counting with confidence on a victory which they believed he would not gain; and it was time-serving, because living in the near neighborhood of the Midianite sheiks, they dreaded the future vengeance of those roving chiefs. This contumelious manner of acting was heartless and disgraceful in people who were of Israelitish blood. <div eID="gen3099" type="x-p"/>
entries.6a209c4fdaa2912364aa3b5e930b09bd0ae51cb2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2300"/><div sID="gen3100" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2300"/><hi type="bold">7. I will tear your flesh with the thorns of the wilderness and with briers--</hi>a cruel torture, to which captives were often subjected in ancient times, by having thorns and briers placed on their naked bodies and pressed down by sledges, or heavy implements of husbandry being dragged over them. <div eID="gen3100" type="x-p"/>
entries.6ff80d0c49fe67509e81ecdab13834dc96636489: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2301"/><div sID="gen3101" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2301"/><hi type="bold">8. he went up thence to Penuel, and spake unto them likewise--</hi>a neighboring city, situated also in the territory of Gad, near the Jabbok, and honored with this name by Jacob (<reference osisRef="Gen.32.30">Ge 32:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.32.31">31</reference>). <div eID="gen3101" type="x-p"/>
entries.ace55640cb6bed388b8cb775f83a51ede40da67a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2302"/><div sID="gen3102" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2302"/><hi type="bold">9. he spake ..., When I come again in peace, I will break down this tower--</hi>Intent on the pursuit, and afraid of losing time, he postponed the merited vengeance till his return. His confident anticipation of a triumphant return evinces the strength of his faith; and his specific threat was probably provoked by some proud and presumptuous boast, that in their lofty watchtower the Penuelites would set him at defiance. <div eID="gen3102" type="x-p"/>
entries.7c91e95383583ea13cd10488ccb568212d69448a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2303"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Judg.8.10-Judg.8.27">Jud 8:10-27</reference>. Zebah and Zalmunna Taken.</title> <div sID="gen3103" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2303"/><hi type="bold">10. Now Zebah and Zalmunna were in Karkor--</hi>a town on the eastern confines of Gad. The wreck of the Midianite army halted there. <div eID="gen3103" type="x-p"/>
entries.26585b9c33af8dcb3a0d87631bbc534729484d6b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2304"/><div sID="gen3104" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2304"/><hi type="bold">11. Gideon went up by the way of them that dwelt in tents on the east--</hi>He tracked the fugitives across the mountain range of Gilead to the northeast of the Jabbok, and there came upon them unexpectedly while they were resting secure among their own nomadic tribes. Jogbehah is supposed to be Ramoth-gilead; and, therefore, the Midianites must have found refuge at or near Abela, "Abel-cheramim," "the plain of the vineyards." <div eID="gen3104" type="x-p"/>
entries.1ed418a9356ed335199eadee83c346d026629553: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2305"/><div sID="gen3105" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2305"/><hi type="bold">12. when Zebah and Zalmunna fled, he pursued after them--</hi>A third conflict took place. His arrival at their last quarters, which was by an unwonted path, took the fugitives by surprise, and the conquest of the Midianite horde was there completed. <div eID="gen3105" type="x-p"/>
entries.434d4b4d3647666b94a2c9b4dac5373f0feaadce: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2306"/><div sID="gen3106" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2306"/><hi type="bold">13. Gideon returned from battle before the sun was up--</hi>He seems to have returned by a nearer route to Succoth, for what is rendered in our version "before the sun was up," means "the heights of Heres, the sun-hills." <div eID="gen3106" type="x-p"/>
entries.181a903bf88466c1a374fc04471b073b0a0e67f2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2307"/><div sID="gen3107" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2307"/><hi type="bold">14. he described--</hi>wrote the names of the seventy princes or elders. It was from them he had received so inhospitable a treatment. <div eID="gen3107" type="x-p"/>
entries.02d83c405b2ac7654966a98f23618367fdd9c5f2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2308"/><div sID="gen3108" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2308"/><hi type="bold">16. he took ... the thorns of the wilderness and briers, and with them he taught the men of Succoth--</hi>By refusing his soldiers refreshment, they had committed a public crime, as well as an act of inhumanity, and were subjected to a horrible punishment, which the great abundance and remarkable size of the thorn bushes, together with the thinness of clothing in the East, has probably suggested. <div eID="gen3108" type="x-p"/>
entries.66848d5ef751f9bb23bb58ac6d382d14a7966242: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2309"/><div sID="gen3109" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2309"/><hi type="bold">18. Then said he unto Zebah and Zalmunna, What manner of men were they whom ye slew at Tabor?--</hi>This was one of the countless atrocities which the Midianite chiefs had perpetrated during their seven years' lawless occupancy. It is noticed now for the first time when their fate was about to be determined.<div eID="gen3109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3110" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">each one resembled the children of a king--</hi>An Orientalism for great beauty, majesty of appearance, uncommon strength, and grandeur of form. <div eID="gen3110" type="x-p"/>
entries.8ee1b1b51e21afaf485dfd8dea9d3b767646d31d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2310"/><div sID="gen3111" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2310"/><hi type="bold">19. They were my brethren, even the sons of my mother--</hi>That is, uterine brothers; but, in all countries where polygamy prevails, "the son of my mother" implies a closeness of relationship and a warmth of affection never awakened by the looser term, "brother." <div eID="gen3111" type="x-p"/>
entries.cee6eae7e9f4e0f3cf1ad4abd2f786d60143d56e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2311"/><div sID="gen3112" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2311"/><hi type="bold">20. he said unto Jether his first-born, Up, and slay them--</hi>The nearest of kin was the blood-avenger; but a magistrate might order any one to do the work of the executioner; and the person selected was always of a rank equal or proportioned to that of the party doomed to suffer (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.29">1Ki 2:29</reference>). Gideon intended, then, by the order to Jether, to put an honor on his son, by employing him to slay two enemies of his country; and on the youth declining, he performed the bloody deed himself. <div eID="gen3112" type="x-p"/>
entries.32c2739f9cdc603d6755a486818c026b9aeca7c9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2312"/><div sID="gen3113" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2312"/><hi type="bold">22-23. the men of Israel said unto Gideon, Rule thou over us ... Gideon said unto them, the Lord shall rule over you--</hi>Their unbounded admiration and gratitude prompted them, in the enthusiasm of the moment, to raise their deliverer to a throne, and to establish a royal dynasty in his house. But Gideon knew too well, and revered too piously the principles of the theocracy, to entertain the proposal for a moment. Personal and family ambition was cheerfully sacrificed to a sense of duty, and every worldly motive was kept in check by a supreme regard to the divine honor. He would willingly act as judge, but the Lord alone was King of Israel. <div eID="gen3113" type="x-p"/>
entries.4f44f83262c32bed74860a957c57979ca35d985b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2313"/><div sID="gen3114" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2313"/><hi type="bold">24-26. Gideon said unto them, I would desire a request of you--</hi>This was the contribution of an earring (singular). As the ancient Arabians (Ishmaelites and Midianites being synonymous terms, <reference osisRef="Gen.37.25">Ge 37:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.37.28">28</reference>) were gorgeously adorned with barbaric pearl and gold, an immense amount of such valuable booty had fallen into the hands of the Israelitish soldiers. The contribution was liberally made, and the quantity of gold given to him is estimated at £3113 sterling. <div eID="gen3114" type="x-p"/>
entries.cc7eafb7dc1f3e6795a5c197c83c412679af90e9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2315"/><div sID="gen3118" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2315"/><hi type="bold">27. Gideon made an ephod thereof, and put it in his city, ... Ophrah--</hi>That no idolatrous use was in view, nor any divisive course from Shiloh contemplated, is manifest from <reference osisRef="Judg.8.33">Jud 8:33</reference>. Gideon proposed, with the gold he received, to make an ephod for his use only as a civil magistrate or ruler, as David did (<reference osisRef="1Chr.15.27">1Ch 15:27</reference>), and a magnificent pectoral or breastplate also. It would seem, from the history, that he was not blamable in making this ephod, as a civil robe or ornament merely, but that it afterward became an object to which religious ideas were attached; whereby it proved a snare, and consequently an evil, by perversion, to Gideon and his house [Taylor, Fragments]. <div eID="gen3118" type="x-p"/>
entries.982dcc1359663e8855e13b0a8e44170e6f36356c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2316"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Judg.8.28">Jud 8:28</reference>. Midian Subdued.</title> <div sID="gen3119" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2316"/><hi type="bold">28. Thus was Midian subdued before the children of Israel--</hi>This invasion of the Arab hordes into Canaan was as alarming and desolating as the irruption of the Huns into Europe. It was the severest scourge ever inflicted upon Israel; and both it and the deliverance under Gideon lived for centuries in the minds of the people (<reference osisRef="Ps.83.11">Psa 83:11</reference>). <chapter eID="Judg.8"/>

entries.413941d6016f0c7f22e3c0e06ed1344784ee362a: <div eID="gen8656" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen8657" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen8658" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen8658" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen8657" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen8659" type="x-p"/> The Ephraimites are angry with Gideon because he did not call them particularly to his assistance; he pacifies them, <reference osisRef="Jdg.8.1-Jdg.8.3">Jdg 8:1-3</reference>. Gideon and his three hundred men pass over Jordan, pursuing the Midianites; and, being faint, ask victuals from the princes of Succoth, but are refused, <reference osisRef="Jdg.8.4-Jdg.8.7">Jdg 8:4-7</reference>. They make the like application to the people of Penuel, and are also refused, <reference osisRef="Jdg.8.8">Jdg 8:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jdg.8.9">Jdg 8:9</reference>. Gideon defeats Zebah and Zalmunna, the two kings of Midian, and takes them prisoners, <reference osisRef="Jdg.8.10-Jdg.8.12">Jdg 8:10-12</reference>. He chastises the men of Succoth and Penuel, <reference osisRef="Jdg.8.13-Jdg.8.17">Jdg 8:13-17</reference>. He slays Zebah and Zalmunna, who had killed his brethren, <reference osisRef="Jdg.8.18-Jdg.8.21">Jdg 8:18-21</reference>. The Israelites offer him the kingdom, which he refuses, <reference osisRef="Jdg.8.22">Jdg 8:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jdg.8.23">Jdg 8:23</reference>. He requires from them the gold rings which they had taken from the Ishmaelites, and makes an ephod, which he sets up at Ophrah; and it became an instrument of idolatry, <reference osisRef="Jdg.8.24-Jdg.8.27">Jdg 8:24-27</reference>. The land enjoys peace forty years; Gideon dies, having seventy-one sons, <reference osisRef="Jdg.8.28-Jdg.8.32">Jdg 8:28-32</reference>. The Israelites fall into idolatry, and forget their obligations to Gideon's family, <reference osisRef="Jdg.8.33-Jdg.8.35">Jdg 8:33-35</reference>. <div eID="gen8659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8660" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen8660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8661" type="x-p"/> The men of Ephraim said - This account is no doubt displaced; for what is mentioned here could not have taken place till the return of Gideon from the pursuit of the Midianites; for he had not yet passed Jordan, <reference osisRef="Jdg.8.4">Jdg 8:4</reference>. And it was when he was beyond that river that the Ephraimites brought the heads of Oreb and Zeeb to him, <reference osisRef="Jdg.7.25">Jdg 7:25</reference>.
entries.93e8d3bc4e97093982b424e5ca92e85ef135be15: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen8661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8662" type="x-p"/> Is not the gleaning, etc. - That is, The Ephraimites have performed more important services than Gideon and his men; and he supports the assertion by observing that it was they who took the two Midianitish generals, having discomfited their hosts at the passes of Jordan.
entries.ff831ac01507c2694c8d52398d717da7bef58e1f: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen8662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8663" type="x-p"/> Then their anger was abated - A soft answer turneth away wrath. He might have said that he could place but little dependence on his brethren when, through faint-heartedness, 22,000 left him at one time; but he passed this by, and took a more excellent way.
entries.56a72874f011389e8ae6275e5f42c97fd5f1764a: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen8663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8664" type="x-p"/> Faint, yet pursuing - The Vulgate paraphrases this, et prae lassitudine, fugientes persequi non poterant; "and, through fatigue, unable to pursue the fugitives."
entries.64ce3e56ebda7dc04a5fbb017127c6a6c5937f9e: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen8664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8665" type="x-p"/> Give, I pray you, loaves of bread - As Gideon was engaged in the common cause of Israel, he had a right to expect succor from the people at large. His request to the men of Succoth and Penuel was both just and reasonable.
entries.97297f3a82e75684275058fcc12a2d05be2d2c82: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen8665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8666" type="x-p"/> Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna now in thine hand - They feared to help Gideon, lest, if he should be overpowered, the Midianites would revenge it upon them; and they dared not trust God.
entries.b5e790c277456446cbd00046c7dfa3af0915bbdd: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen8666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8667" type="x-p"/> I will tear your flesh - What this punishment consisted in I cannot say; it must mean a severe punishment: as if he had said, I will thresh your flesh with briers and thorns, as corn is threshed out with threshing instruments; or, Ye shall be trodden down under the feet of my victorious army, as the corn is trodden out with the feet of the ox. Succoth was beyond Jordan, in the tribe of Gad. Penuel was also in the same tribe, and not far distant from Succoth.
entries.bdc84a256479d8a129d1e220999ae8ace48e619f: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen8667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8668" type="x-p"/> I will break down this tower - Probably they had not only denied him, but insultingly pointed to a tower in which their chief defense lay; and intimated to him that he might do his worst, for they could amply defend themselves.
entries.c1ccbf2bb837ecb7fe7f9566e484246feac46e45: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen8668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8669" type="x-p"/> Zebah and Zalmunna were in Karkor - If this were a place, it is nowhere else mentioned in Scripture. Some contend that קרקר karkor signifies rest; and thus the Vulgate understood it: Zebah and Zalmunna requiescebant, rested, with all their army. And this seems the most likely, for it is said, <reference osisRef="Jdg.8.11">Jdg 8:11</reference>, that Gideon smote the host, for the host was secure.
entries.e283fbe2819a1a6b3cb73b16cd6ed9ed2c4eda75: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen8669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8670" type="x-p"/> Returned from battle before the sun was up - This does not appear to be a proper translation of מלמעלה החרס milmaaleh hechares. It should be rendered from the ascent of Chares: this is the reading of the Septuagint, the Syriac, and the Arabic.
entries.87315f2d4352fdf99fbbcde8f1cfd3a45aaf6a82: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen8670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8671" type="x-p"/> He described unto him the princes of Succoth - The young man probably gave him the names of seventy persons, the chief men of Succoth, who were those who were most concerned in refusing him and his men the refreshment he requested.
entries.d8a03fbc77b4af0051b12b21f0e83aec16c93acf: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen8671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8672" type="x-p"/> He taught the men of Succoth - Instead of וידע he taught, Houbigant reads וידש he tore; and this is not only agreeable to what Gideon had threatened, <reference osisRef="Jdg.8.7">Jdg 8:7</reference>, but is supported by the Vulgate, Septuagint, Chaldee, Syriac, and Arabic. The Hebrew text might have been easily corrupted in this place by the change of ש shin into ע ain, letters very similar to each other.
entries.d44a545886a283a65d6b3a644ad6153d1b5b435e: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen8672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8673" type="x-p"/> What manner of men were they whom ye slew at Tabor? - We have no antecedent to this question; and are obliged to conjecture one: it seems as if Zebah and Zalmunna had massacred the family of Gideon, while he was absent on this expedition. Gideon had heard some confused account of it, and now questions them concerning the fact. They boldly acknowledge it, and describe the persons whom they slew, by which he found they were his own brethren. This determines him to avenge their death by slaying the Midianitish kings, whom he otherwise was inclined to save. He might have heard that his brethren had been taken prisoners, and might have hoped to have exchanged them for the kings now in his hand; but when he found they had been all slain, he decrees the death of their murderers. There is something in this account similar to that in the 12th Aeneis of Virgil: - When Turnus was overthrown, and supplicated for his life, and Aeneas was inclined to spare him; he saw the belt of his friend Pallas, whom Turnus had slain, and which he now wore as a trophy: this immediately determined the Trojan to sacrifice the life of Turnus to the manes of his friend. The story is well told: - <div eID="gen8673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8674" type="x-p"/> Stetit acer in armis <div eID="gen8674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8675" type="x-p"/> Aeneas, volvens oculos, dextramque repressit. <div eID="gen8675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8676" type="x-p"/> Et jam jamque magis cunctantem flectere sermo <div eID="gen8676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8677" type="x-p"/> Coeperat: infelix humero cum apparuit ingens <div eID="gen8677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8678" type="x-p"/> Balteus, et notis fulserunt cingula bullis <div eID="gen8678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8679" type="x-p"/> Pallantis pueri; victum quem vulnere Turnus <div eID="gen8679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8680" type="x-p"/> Straverat, atque humeris inimicum insigne gerebat. <div eID="gen8680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8681" type="x-p"/> Ille oculis postquam saevi monumenta doloris <div eID="gen8681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8682" type="x-p"/> Exuviasque hausit: furiis accensus et ira <div eID="gen8682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8683" type="x-p"/> Terribilis: Tune hinc spoliis indute meorum <div eID="gen8683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8684" type="x-p"/> Eripiare mihi? - Pallas, te hoc vulnere Pallas <div eID="gen8684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8685" type="x-p"/> Immolat; et poenam scelerato ex sanguine sumit. <div eID="gen8685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8686" type="x-p"/> Hoc dicens furrum adverso sub pectore condit Fervidus. <div eID="gen8686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8687" type="x-p"/> Virg. Aen. lib. xii., ver. 938. "In deep suspense the Trojan seem'd to stand, <div eID="gen8687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8688" type="x-p"/> And, just prepared to strike, repress'd his hand. <div eID="gen8688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8689" type="x-p"/> He roll'd his eyes, and every moment felt <div eID="gen8689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8690" type="x-p"/> His manly soul with more compassion melt. <div eID="gen8690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8691" type="x-p"/> When, casting down a casual glance, he spied <div eID="gen8691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8692" type="x-p"/> The golden belt that glitter'd on his side; <div eID="gen8692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8693" type="x-p"/> The fatal spoils which haughty Turnus tore <div eID="gen8693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8694" type="x-p"/> From dying Pallas, and in triumph wore. <div eID="gen8694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8695" type="x-p"/> Then roused anew to wrath, he loudly cries, (Flames, while he spoke, came flashing from his eyes), <div eID="gen8695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8696" type="x-p"/> Traitor! dost thou! dost thou to grace pretend, <div eID="gen8696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8697" type="x-p"/> Clad, as thou art, in trophies of my friend? - <div eID="gen8697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8698" type="x-p"/> To his sad soul a grateful offering go; 'Tis Pallas, Pallas gives this deadly blow. <div eID="gen8698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8699" type="x-p"/> He rais'd his arm aloft; and at the word, <div eID="gen8699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8700" type="x-p"/> Deep in his bosom drove the shining sword." <div eID="gen8700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8701" type="x-p"/> Dryden. <div eID="gen8701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8702" type="x-p"/> The same principle impels Gideon to slay Zebah and Zalmunna which induced Aeneas to kill Turnus: and perhaps the ornaments which he took from their camels' necks, <reference osisRef="Jdg.8.21">Jdg 8:21</reference>, were some of the spoils of his slaughtered brethren.
entries.79160dcc7308fbfd32c30ceef5a5be3f083f6e6c: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen8702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8703" type="x-p"/> He said unto Jether his first-born - By the ancient laws of war, prisoners taken in war might be either slain, sold, or kept for slaves. To put a captive enemy to death no executioner was required. Gideon slays Zebah and Zalmunna with his own hand. So Samuel is said to have hewn Agag in pieces, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.33">1Sam 15:33</reference>. Benaiah slew Joab, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.25">1Kgs 2:25</reference>. Saul orders his guards to slay the priests who had contributed to the escape of David, <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.17">1Sam 22:17</reference>; and David caused one of his attendants to slay the Amalekite who pretended to have slain Saul, <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.15">2Sam 1:15</reference>.
entries.8e8787f6576a3e539124892f537f1565535297bf: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen8703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8704" type="x-p"/> Then Zebah and Zalmunna said, Rise, thou, and fall upon us - It was disgraceful to fall by the hands of a child; and the death occasioned by the blows of such a person must be much more lingering and tormenting. Some have even employed children to despatch captives. Civilis, a Roman knight, headed a revolt of the Gauls against Rome, in the year of the city 824. Of him Tacitus says, Hist. lib. iv., c. 61: Ferebatur parvulo filio quosdam captivorum sagittis jaculisque puerilibus figendos obtulisse: "He is said to have given to his little son some prisoners, as butts to be shot at with little darts and arrows." This was for their greater torment and dishonor; and to inure his child to blood! Could any thing like this have been the design of Gideon? <div eID="gen8704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8705" type="x-p"/> The ornaments that were on their camels' necks. - The heads, necks, bodies, and legs of camels, horses, and elephants, are highly ornamented in the eastern countries, and indeed this was common, from the remotest antiquity, in all countries. Virgil refers to it as a thing long before his time, and thus describes the horses given by King Latinus to the ambassadors of Aeneas. - Aen. lib. vii., ver. 274. <div eID="gen8705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8706" type="x-p"/> Haec effatus equos numero pater eligit omni. <div eID="gen8706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8707" type="x-p"/> Stabant tercentum nitidi in praesepibus altis: <div eID="gen8707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8708" type="x-p"/> Omnibus extemplo Teucris jubet ordine duci <div eID="gen8708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8709" type="x-p"/> Instratos ostro alipedes pictisque tapetis. Aurea pectoribus demissa monilia pendent: Tecti auro fulvum mandunt sub dentibus aurum. "He said, and order'd steeds to mount the band: In lofty stalls three hundred coursers stand; Their shining sides with crimson cover'd o'er; The sprightly steeds embroider'd trappings wore, With golden chains, refulgent to behold: Gold were their bridles, and they champ'd on gold." <div eID="gen8709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8710" type="x-p"/> Pitt. <div eID="gen8710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8711" type="x-p"/> Instead of ornaments, the Septuagint translate τους μηνισκους, the crescents or half-moons; and this is followed by the Syriac and Arabic. The worship of the moon was very ancient; and, with that of the sun, constituted the earliest idolatry of mankind. We learn from <reference osisRef="Jdg.8.24">Jdg 8:24</reference> that the Ishmaelites, or Arabs, as they are termed by the Targum, Syriac, and Arabic, had golden ear-rings, and probably a crescent in each; for it is well known that the Ishmaelites, and the Arabs who descended from them, were addicted very early to the worship of the moon; and so attached were they to this superstition, that although Mohammed destroyed the idolatrous use of the crescent, yet it was universally borne in their ensigns, and on the tops of their mosques, as well as in various ornaments.
entries.f0894d30ce212e81bd391312862cb32de3b80f04: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen8711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8712" type="x-p"/> Rule thou over us, both thou, and thy son, and thy son's son - That is, Become our king, and let the crown be hereditary in thy family. What a weak, foolish, and inconstant people were these! As yet their government was a theocracy; and now, dazzled with the success of a man who was only an instrument in the hands of God to deliver them from their enemies, they wish to throw off the Divine yoke, and shackle themselves with an unlimited hereditary monarchy! An unlimited monarchy is a curse; a limited monarchy may be a blessing: the latter may be an appointment of God; the former never can. Those who cast off their allegiance to their Maker, are guilty of folly and extravagance of every kind.
entries.db2b9ec505092808153e8aa20849b01208443528: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen8712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8713" type="x-p"/> The Lord shall rule over you - Few with such power at their command would have acted as Gideon. His speech calls them back to their first principles, and should have excited in them both shame and contrition. How different is this speech from that of Oliver Cromwell when the commons offered him the crown of England!
entries.b7c14bacdbde7dc0329d6d8764f85146e19a7f6d: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen8713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8714" type="x-p"/> Give me every man the ear-rings of his prey - The spoils taken from their enemies in this warfare. This is a transaction very like to that of the Israelites and Aaron; when they brought him their golden ear-rings, out of which he made the molten calf, <reference osisRef="Exo.32.2">Exo 32:2</reference>, etc. Whether Gideon designed this ephod for an instrument of worship, or merely as a trophy, is not very clear. It is most likely that he had intended to establish a place of worship at Ophrah; and he took this occasion to provide the proper sacerdotal vestments.
entries.eb9412bd3609400ba7e11264aed9dcb357bf1146: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen8714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8715" type="x-p"/> The weight of the golden ear-rings - was a thousand and seven hundred shekels of gold - Taking the shekel at half an ounce weight, the sum of the gold collected in ear-rings was seventy pounds ten ounces; and worth, as gold now rates, about 3,100 sterling. This computation of the weight of the golden ear-rings, taken from the slaughtered Ishmaelites, will bring to the reader's mind the slaughter of the Roman knights by the Carthaginians at the battle of Cannae, from whose spoils Hannibal sent three bushels of gold rings to the city of Carthage!
entries.2cf0743fdc714b57e484c7b09c8c7389644144c1: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen8715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8716" type="x-p"/> Gideon made an ephod thereof - That is, he made an ephod out of this mass of gold; but he could not employ it all in making this one garment, for it is not likely that any man could wear a coat of nearly one hundred pounds weight. It is likely that he made a whole tabernacle service in miniature out of this gold. <div eID="gen8716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8717" type="x-p"/> All Israel went thither a whoring after it - This form of speech often occurs, and has been often explained. The whole Jewish nation is represented as being united to God as a wife is to her husband. Any act of idolatry is considered as a breach of their covenant with God, as an act of whoredom is the breach of the marriage agreement between man and wife. God calls himself the husband of the Jewish nation, and their idolatries acts of whoredom, adultery, and fornication. All Israel paid idolatrous worship to the ephod or sacerdotal establishment made by Gideon at Ophrah, and this is called going a whoring after it; see on <reference osisRef="Jdg.8.33">Jdg 8:33</reference> (note). For a description of the ephod, see <reference osisRef="Exo.25.7">Exo 25:7</reference> (note); and for the other garments of the priests, see <reference osisRef="Exo.28.4">Exo 28:4</reference> (note), etc.
entries.41364d6bf4a46acce2ebc0aff474fd2dea6268aa: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen8717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8718" type="x-p"/> Forty years in the days of Gideon - The Midianites were so completely humbled that they could make head no more against Israel during the forty years in which the government of Gideon lasted.
entries.9c989117aecdf22339ecb9feb248c3a3ea82ca52: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen8718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8719" type="x-p"/> His concubine - A lawful but secondary wife, whose children could not inherit. <div eID="gen8719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8720" type="x-p"/> Whose name he called Abimelech - That is, my father is king, or my father hath reigned. This name was doubtless given by the mother, and so it should be understood here; she wished to raise her son to the supreme government, and therefore gave him a name which might serve to stimulate him to seek that which she hoped he should enjoy in his father's right. See the following chapter, Judges 9 (note).
