entries.e929f4e844e80f9e422dcc6196e6f2f0f5c5921a: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen8720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8721" type="x-p"/> Gideon - died in a good old age - Supposed to have been A.M. 2799; b.c. 1205.
entries.65df1aea8dedfeaf14bb5aeed13691d9161b573d: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen8721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8722" type="x-p"/> A whoring after Baalim - This term has probably a different meaning here from what it has <reference osisRef="Jdg.8.7">Jdg 8:7</reference>; for it is very likely that in most parts of the pagan worship there were many impure rites, so that going a whoring after Baalim may be taken in a literal sense. <div eID="gen8722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8723" type="x-p"/> Baal-berith - Literally, the lord of the covenant; the same as Jupiter faederis, or Mercury, among the Romans; the deity whose business it was to preside over compacts, leagues, treaties, covenants, etc. Some of the versions understand it as if the Israelites had made a covenant or agreement to have Baal for their god; so the Vulgate: Percusseruntque cum Baal faedus, ut esset eis in deum.
entries.e2035acc5ea7de639bbd3c20f7f6be78199450d2: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen8723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8724" type="x-p"/> Remembered not the Lord their God - They attributed their deliverance to some other cause, and did not give him the glory of their salvation.
entries.57550d552f027b8a99908417e9dd75d6bcf0e8ac: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen8724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8725" type="x-p"/> Neither showed they kindness to the house of - Gideon - They were both unthankful and unholy. Though they had the clearest proofs of God's power and goodness before their eyes, yet they forgot him. And although they were under the greatest obligations to Gideon, and were once so sensible of them that they offered to settle the kingdom on him and his family, yet they forgot him also; for, becoming foes to God, they could not be friends to Man. Jerubbaal, namely, Gideon. - This is improper; it should be Jerubbaal Gideon, as we say Simon Peter, or call any man by his Christian name and surname. <div eID="gen8725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8726" type="x-p"/> The ancients, particularly St. Ambrose and Augustine, have endeavored to find out a parallel between our blessed Lord and Gideon. We have already seen what Origen has made of the whole account, who is followed in the main by the above Latin fathers. As I believe no such parallel was intended by the Spirit of God, I must be excused from going into their details. It is no credit either to Christ or Christianity to be compared to such persons and their transactions. <div eID="gen8726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8727" type="x-p"/> 1. Of Gideon the most we can say is that which the angel said, he was a mighty man of valor. <div eID="gen8727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8728" type="x-p"/> 2. He was also a true patriot, he loved his country, and hazarded his life for it; and yet he would not stir till he had the most incontestable proofs that God would, by his supernatural assistance, make him victorious. <div eID="gen8728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8729" type="x-p"/> 3. He was most evidently disinterested, and void of ambition; he refused the kingdom when it was offered to him and to his heirs after him. But, consistently with the belief he had in God, he could not accept it, as this would have been a complete alteration of the Jewish constitution, which acknowledged no ruler but God himself. <div eID="gen8729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8730" type="x-p"/> 4. His motive in making the ephod is not well understood; probably it was done with no reprehensible design. But the act was totally wrong; he had no Divine authority to make such an innovation in the religious worship of his country. The ark was at Shechem; and there was the proper and only accredited priest. The act therefore can never be excused, whatever may be said of his motive. <div eID="gen8730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8731" type="x-p"/> 5. His private character does not appear to have been very exemplary; he had many wives, and seventy sons by them, besides one by a concubine, which he kept at Shechem, where he was often obliged to go as judge, for the purpose of administering justice. In short, there is scarcely a trait in his character worthy to be compared with any thing in the conduct of the Redeemer of mankind. <div eID="gen8731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8732" type="x-p"/> 6. Parallels to Christ, and the work of his Spirit in the salvation of men, have been diligently sought in the sacred writings, by both commentators and preachers; and we have had voluminous treaties on types and antitypes; and how little has sound doctrine or true piety derived from them! They have often served to unsettle the former, and have been rather inimical than favorable to the interests of the latter. When the Spirit of God says such things are types and such things are allegories, it is our duty to believe and examine; when men produce their types and metaphors, it may be our duty to doubt, be suspicious, and pass on.  <chapter eID="Judg.8"/> <div eID="gen8732" type="x-p"/>

entries.8e7066dd0ae5c94f96f69cc8d58b7fb65d20216d: Jdg 8:1-3 <div eID="gen3273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3274" type="x-p"/> When the Ephraimites met with Gideon, after they had smitten the Midianites at Oreb and Zeeb, and were pursuing them farther, they said to him, “<hi type="italic">What is the thing that thou hast done to us</hi> (i.e., what is the reason for your having done this to us), <hi type="italic">not to call us when thou wentest forth to make war upon Midian? And they did chide with him sharply,</hi>” less from any dissatisfied longing for booty, than from injured pride or jealousy, because Gideon had made war upon the enemy and defeated them without the co-operation of this tribe, which was striving for the leadership. Gideon’s reply especially suggests the idea of injured ambition: “<hi type="italic">What have I now done like you?</hi>” sc., as if I had done as great things as you. “<hi type="italic">Is not the gleaning of Ephraim better than the vintage of Abiezer?</hi>” The gleaning of Ephraim is the victory gained over the flying Midianites. Gideon declares this to be better than the vintage of Abiezer, i.e., the victory obtained by him the Abiezrite with his 300 men, because the Ephraimites had slain two Midianitish princes. The victory gained by the Ephraimites must indeed have been a very important one, as it is mentioned by Isaiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.26">Isa 10:26</reference>) as a great blow of the Lord upon Midian. “<hi type="italic">And what could I do like you?</hi>” i.e., could I accomplish such great deeds as you? “<hi type="italic">Then their anger turned away from him</hi>.” רוּח, the breathing of the nose, snorting, hence “<hi type="italic">anger</hi>,” as in <reference osisRef="Isa.25.4">Isa 25:4</reference>, etc. <div eID="gen3274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3275" type="x-p"/> Pursuit and Complete Overthrow of the Midianites. - That the Midianites whom God had delivered into his hand might be utterly destroyed, Gideon pursued those who had escaped across the Jordan, till he overtook them on the eastern boundary of Gilead and smote them there.
entries.69d5d0e6316489723bad9e2de2f84017ab54484c: Jdg 8:4-5 <div eID="gen3275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3276" type="x-p"/> When he came to the Jordan with his three hundred men, who were exhausted with the pursuit, he asked the inhabitants of Succoth for loaves of bread for the people in his train. So far as the construction is concerned, the words from עבר to ורדפים form a circumstantial clause inserted as a parenthesis into the principal sentence, and subordinate to it: “<hi type="italic">When Gideon came to the Jordan, passing over he and the three hundred men ... then he said to the men of Succoth</hi>.” “<hi type="italic">Exhausted and pursuing</hi>,” i.e., exhausted with pursuing. The <hi type="italic">vav</hi> is explanatory, <hi type="italic">lit</hi>. “and indeed pursuing,” for “because he pursued.” The rendering πεινῶντες adopted by the lxx in the <hi type="italic">Cod</hi>. <hi type="italic">Alex</hi>. is merely an arbitrary rendering of the word רדפים, and without any critical worth. Gideon had crossed the Jordan, therefore, somewhere in the neighbourhood of Succoth. Succoth was upon the eastern side of the valley of the Jordan (<reference osisRef="Josh.13.27">Jos 13:27</reference>), not opposite to Bethshean, but, according to <reference osisRef="Gen.33.17">Gen 33:17</reference>, on the south side of the Jabbok (Zerka).
entries.ee9e57be99711179d518c2ae1afcb78991c41b7a: Jdg 8:6 <div eID="gen3276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3277" type="x-p"/> The princes of Succoth, however, showed so little sympathy and nationality of feeling, that instead of taking part of the attack upon the enemies of Israel, they even refused to supply bread to refresh their brethren of the western tribes who were exhausted with the pursuit of the foe. They said (the sing. ויּאמר may be explained on the ground that one spoke in the name of all: see <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §319, <hi type="italic">a</hi>.), “<hi type="italic">Is the fist of Zebah and Zalmunna already in thy hand </hi>(power), <hi type="italic">that we should give thine army bread?</hi>” In these words there is not only an expression of cowardice, or fear of the vengeance which the Midianites might take when they returned upon those who had supported Gideon and his host, but contempt of the small force which Gideon had, as if it were impossible for him to accomplish anything at all against the foe; and in this contempt they manifested their utter want of confidence in God.
entries.746ab6395cf8a39dffa4bd202c046277004d14a1: Jdg 8:7 <div eID="gen3277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3278" type="x-p"/> Gideon threatened them, therefore, with severe chastisement in the event of a victorious return. “<hi type="italic">If Jehovah give Zebah and Zalmunna into my hand, I will thresh your flesh</hi> (your body) <hi type="italic">with desert thorns and thistles</hi>.” The verb דּוּשׁ, constructed with a double accusative (see <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §283, <hi type="italic"></hi>.), is used in a figurative sense: “to thresh,” in other words, to punish severely. “Thorns of the desert” as strong thorns, as the desert is the natural soil for thorn-bushes. The ἁπ. λεγ. בּרקנים also signifies prickly plants, according to the early versions and the Rabbins, probably “such as grow upon stony ground” (<hi type="italic">Bertheau</hi>). The explanation “threshing machines with stones or flints underneath them,” which was suggested by <hi type="italic">J. D. Michaelis</hi> and <hi type="italic">Celsius</hi>, and adopted by <hi type="italic">Gesenius</hi>, cannot be sustained.
entries.a2e393d0b17867c591322c05ec3f88856c701b47: Jdg 8:8-9 <div eID="gen3278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3279" type="x-p"/> The inhabitants of Pnuel on the north bank of the Jabbok (see at Gen 32:24.) behaved in the same churlish manner to Gideon, and for this he also threatened them: “If I return in peace,” i.e., unhurt, “<hi type="italic">I will destroy this tower</hi>” (probably the castle of Pnuel).
entries.ef4ff5bf09e3ab563cd0259556d6365ab4ee4a97: Jdg 8:10-12 <div eID="gen3279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3280" type="x-p"/> The Midianitish kings were at <hi type="italic">Karkor</hi> with all the remnant of their army, about fifteen thousand men, a hundred and twenty thousand having already fallen. Gideon followed them thither by the road of the dwellers in tents on the east of <hi type="italic">Nobah</hi> and <hi type="italic">Jogbeha</hi>; and falling upon them unawares, smote the whole camp, which thought itself quite secure, and took the two kings prisoners, after discomfiting all the camp. The situation of <hi type="italic">Karkor</hi>, which is only mentioned here, cannot be determined with certainty. The statement of <hi type="italic">Eusebius</hi> and <hi type="italic">Jerome</hi> (<hi type="italic">Onom. s. v</hi>. Καρκὰ, <hi type="italic">Carcar</hi>), that it was the castle of <hi type="italic">Carcaria</hi>, a day’s journey from <hi type="italic">Petra</hi>, is decidedly wrong, since this castle is much too far to the south, as <hi type="italic">Gesenius</hi> (Thes. p. 1210) has shown. <hi type="italic">Karkor</hi> cannot have been very far from <hi type="italic">Nobah</hi> and Jogbeha. These two places are probably preserved in the ruins of <hi type="italic">Nowakis</hi> and <hi type="italic">Jebeiha</hi>, on the north-west of <hi type="italic">Ammân</hi> (<hi type="italic">Rabbath-ammon</hi>; see at Num 21:31). Now, as <hi type="italic">Burckhardt</hi> (Syr. p. 612) also mentions a ruin in the neighbourhood, called <hi type="italic">Karkagheisch</hi>, on the left of the road from Szalt to Ammân, and at the most an hour and a half to the north-west of Ammân, <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> (on Num 32:42) is inclined to regard this ruin as <hi type="italic">Karkor</hi>. If this supposition could be proved to be correct, Gideon would have fallen upon the camp of the enemy from the north-east. For “<hi type="italic">the way of the dwellers in tents on the east of Nobah and Jogbeha</hi>” cannot well be any other than the way which ran to the east of Nobah and Jogbeha, past the most easterly frontier city of the Gadites, to the nomads who dwelt in the desert. באללים השּׁכוּני has the article attached to the governing noun, which may easily be explained in this instance from the intervening preposition. The passive participle שׁכוּן has an intransitive force (see <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §149, <hi type="italic">a</hi>.). The verb החריד in the circumstantial clause acquires the force of the pluperfect from the context. When he had startled the camp out of its security, having alarmed it by his unexpected attack, he succeeded in taking the two kings prisoners. <div eID="gen3280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3281" type="x-p"/> Punishment of the Towns of Succoth and Pnuel, and Execution of the Captures Kings of Midian.
entries.a390bedb8859219a0ce7b6d6f217cedc5ba0acc3: Jdg 8:13-14 <div eID="gen3281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3282" type="x-p"/> Gideon returned victorious from the war, החרס מלמעלה, “<hi type="italic">from by the ascent </hi>(<hi type="italic">or mountain road</hi>) <hi type="italic">of Hecheres</hi>,” a place in front of the town of Succoth, with which we are not acquainted. This is the rendering adopted by the lxx, the Peshito, and the Arabic; but the rest of the early translators have merely guessed at the meaning. The <hi type="italic">Chaldee</hi>, which has been followed by the <hi type="italic">Rabbins</hi> and <hi type="italic">Luther</hi>, has rendered it “before sunset,” in utter opposition to the rules of the language; for although <hi type="italic">cheres</hi> is a word used poetically to denote the sun, מעלה cannot mean the setting of the sun. <hi type="italic">Aquila</hi> and <hi type="italic">Symmachus</hi>, on the other hand, confound חרס with הרים. - Gideon laid hold of a young man of the people of Succoth, and got him to write down for him the princes and elders (magistrates and rulers) of the city, - in all seventy-seven men. ויּכתּב ויּשׁאלהוּ is a short expression for “he asked him the names of the princes and elders of the city, and the boy wrote them down.” אליו, <hi type="italic">lit</hi>. to him, i.e., for him.
entries.0bc30a00b7f121671a00e17338be9edf8c1c2f17: Jdg 8:15-16 <div eID="gen3282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3283" type="x-p"/> Gideon then reproached the elders with the insult they had offered him (Jdg 8:6), and had them punished with desert thorns and thistles. “<hi type="italic">Men of Succoth</hi>” (<hi type="italic">Jdg 8:15</hi> and <hi type="italic">Jdg 8:16</hi>) is a general expression for “elders of Succoth” (<hi type="italic">Jdg 8:16</hi>); and elders a general term applied to all the representatives of the city, including the princes. אתי חרפתּם אשׁר, with regard to whom ye have despised me. אשׁר is the accusative of the more distant or second object, not the subject, as <hi type="italic">Stud</hi>. supposes. “<hi type="italic">And he taught the men of Succoth</hi> (i.e., caused them to know, made them feel, punished them) with them (the thorns).” There is no good ground for doubting the correctness of the reading ויּדע. The free renderings of the lxx, <hi type="italic">Vulg</hi>., etc., are destitute of critical worth; and <hi type="italic">Bertheau's</hi> assertion, that if it were the <hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi> it would be written יודע, is proved to be unfounded by the defective writing in Num 16:5; Job 32:7.
entries.125d071cc5929c59107c87cd3764c10e6651522e: Jdg 8:17 <div eID="gen3283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3284" type="x-p"/> Gideon also inflicted upon Pnuel the punishment threatened in Jdg 8:9. The punishment inflicted by Gideon upon both the cities was well deserved in all respects, and was righteously executed. The inhabitants of these cities had not only acted treacherously to Israel as far as they could, from the most selfish interests, in a holy conflict for the glory of the Lord and the freedom of His people, but in their contemptuous treatment of Gideon and his host they had poured contempt upon the Lord, who had shown them to be His own soldiers before the eyes of the whole nation by the victory which He had given them over the innumerable army of the foe. Having been called by the Lord to be the deliverer and judge of Israel, it was Gideon’s duty to punish the faithless cities.
entries.376fc8757ec3d82db1cf7d2d2464444fb1b3d7f9: Jdg 8:18-21 <div eID="gen3284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3285" type="x-p"/> After punishing these cities, Gideon repaid the two kings of Midian, who had been taken prisoners, according to their doings. From the judicial proceedings instituted with regard to them (Jdg 8:18, Jdg 8:19), we learn that these kings had put the brothers of Gideon to death, and apparently not in open fight; but they had murdered them in an unrighteous and cruel manner. And Gideon made them atone for this with their own lives, according to the strict <hi type="italic">jus talionis</hi>. איפה, in Jdg 8:18, does not mean <hi type="italic">where</hi>? but “<hi type="italic">in what condition, of what form, were the men whom he slew at Tabor?</hi>” i.e., either in the city of Tabor or at Mount Tabor (see Jdg 4:6, and <reference osisRef="Josh.19.22">Jos 19:22</reference>). The kings replied: “<hi type="italic">As thou so they</hi>” (those men), i.e., they were all as stately as thou art, “<hi type="italic">every one like the form of kings’ sons.</hi>” אחד, one, for every one, like אחד אישׁ in 2Ki 15:20, or more frequently אישׁ alone. As the men who had been slain were Gideon’s own brothers, he swore to those who had done the deed, i.e., to the two kings, “<hi type="italic">As truly as Jehovah liveth, if ye had let them live I should not have put you to death;</hi>” and then commanded his first-born son Jether to slay them, for the purpose of adding the disgrace of falling by the hand of a boy. “<hi type="italic">But the boy drew not his sword from fear, because he was yet a boy</hi>.” And the kings then said to Gideon, “<hi type="italic">Rise thou and stab us, for as the man so is his strength,</hi>” i.e., such strength does not belong to a boy, but to a man. Thereupon Gideon slew them, and took the little moons upon the necks of their camels as booty. “<hi type="italic">The little moons</hi>” were crescent-shaped ornaments of silver or gold, such as men and women wore upon their necks (see Jdg 8:26, and <reference osisRef="Isa.3.18">Isa 3:18</reference>), and which they also hung upon the necks of camels-a custom still prevalent in Arabia (<hi type="italic">see Schröder, de vestitu mul. hebr</hi>. pp. 39, 40, and <hi type="italic">Wellsted, Reisen</hi> <hi type="italic">in Arab</hi>. i. p. 209).
entries.254e09eba84b44ebcfedb9eb50c421567541c2a3: Jdg 8:22-23 <div eID="gen3285" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3286" type="x-p"/> Gideon’s Remaining Acts, and Death. - Jdg 8:22, Jdg 8:23. As Gideon had so gloriously delivered Israel from the severe and long oppression on the part of the Midianites, the Israelites offered him an hereditary crown. “<hi type="italic">The men of Israel</hi>” were hardly all the twelve tribes, but probably only the northern tribes of the western part of the land already mentioned in Jdg 6:35, who had suffered the most severely from the Midianitish oppression, and had been the first to gather round Gideon to make an attack upon the foe. The temptation to accept the government of Israel was resisted by this warrior of God. “<hi type="italic">Neither I nor my son shall rule over you; Jehovah shall rule over you,</hi>” was his reply to this offer, containing an evident allusion to the destination and constitution of the tribes of Israel as a nation which Jehovah had chosen to be His own possession, and to which He had just made himself known in so conspicuous a manner as their omnipotent Ruler and King. This refusal of the regal dignity on the part of Gideon is not at variance with the fact, that Moses had already foreseen the possibility that at some future time the desire for a king would arise in the nation, and had given them a law for the king expressly designed for such circumstances as these (Deu 17:14.). For Gideon did not decline the honour because Jehovah was King in Israel, i.e., because he regarded an earthly monarchy in Israel as irreconcilable with the heavenly monarchy of Jehovah, but simply because he thought the government of Jehovah in Israel amply sufficient, and did not consider either himself or his sons called to found an earthly monarchy.
entries.acc47b9da7e35a2066fa33178ee754f41e62f9ec: Jdg 8:24 <div eID="gen3286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3287" type="x-p"/> Gideon resisted the temptation to put an earthly crown upon his head, from true fidelity to Jehovah; but he yielded to another temptation, which this appeal on the part of the people really involved, namely, the temptation to secure to himself for the future the position to which the Lord had called and exalted him. The Lord had called him to be the deliverer of Israel by visibly appearing in His angel, and had not only accepted the gift which he offered Him, as a well-pleasing sacrifice, but had also commanded him to build an altar, and by offering an atoning burnt-sacrifice to re-establish the worship of Jehovah in his family and tribe, and to restore the favour of God to His people once more. Lastly, the Lord had made His will known to him again and again; whilst by the glorious victory which He had given to him and to his small band over the powerful army of the foe, He had confirmed him as His chosen servant to be the deliverer and judge of Israel. The relation which Gideon thus sustained to the Lord he imagined that he ought to preserve; and therefore, after declining the royal dignity, he said to the people, “<hi type="italic">I will request of you one request, that ye give me every one the ring that he has received as booty.</hi>” This request the historian explains by adding the remark: “<hi type="italic">for they</hi> (the enemy) <hi type="italic">had golden rings, for they were Ishmaelites,</hi>” from whom therefore the Israelites were able to get an abundance of rings as booty. <hi type="italic">Ishmaelites</hi> is the general name for the nomad tribes of Arabia, to whom the Midianites also belonged (as in <reference osisRef="Gen.37.25">Gen 37:25</reference>).
entries.2409e7d56c30c538134a48eae4d0b62df2dea02e: Jdg 8:25-26 <div eID="gen3287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3288" type="x-p"/> This request of Gideon’s was cheerfully fulfilled: “<hi type="italic">They spread out the cloth</hi> (brought for collecting the rings), <hi type="italic">and threw into it every one the ring that he had received as booty.</hi>” <hi type="italic">Simlah</hi>, the upper garment, was for the most part only a large square piece of cloth. The weight of these golden rings amounted to 1700 shekels, i.e., about 50 lbs., (מן לבד) separate from, i.e., beside, the remaining booty, for which Gideon had not asked, and which the Israelites kept for themselves, viz., the little moons, the ear-pendants (<hi type="italic">netiphoth , lit</hi>. little drops, probably pearl-shaped ear-drops: see <reference osisRef="Isa.3.19">Isa 3:19</reference>), and the purple clothes which were worn by the kings of Midian (i.e., which they had on), and also apart from the neck-bands upon the necks of their camels. Instead of the <hi type="italic">anakoth</hi> or necklaces (Jdg 8:26), the <hi type="italic">saharonim</hi>, or little moons upon the necks of the camels, are mentioned in Jdg 8:21 as the more valuable portion of these necklaces. Even at the present day the Arabs are accustomed to ornament the necks of these animals “with a band of cloth or leather, upon which small shells called cowries are strung or sewed in the form of a crescent. The sheiks add silver ornaments to these, which make a rich booty in time of war” (<hi type="italic">Wellsted</hi>, Reise, i. p. 209). The Midianitish kings had their camels ornamented with golden crescents. This abundance of golden ornaments will not surprise us, when we consider that the Arabs still carry their luxurious tastes for such things to a very great excess. <hi type="italic">Wellsted</hi> (i. p. 224) states that “the women in Omân spend considerable amounts in the purchase of silver ornaments, and their children are literally laden with them. I have sometimes counted fifteen ear-rings upon each side; and the head, breast, arms, and ankles are adorned with the same profusion.” As the Midianitish army consisted of 130,000 men, of whom 15,000 only remained at the commencement of the last engagement, the Israelites may easily have collected 5000 golden rings, or even more, which might weigh 1700 shekels.
entries.e1e431e6859d8f70a4a990ff78a90ec00b4b8ac6: Jdg 8:27 <div eID="gen3288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3289" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">And Gideon made it into an ephod</hi>,” i.e., used the gold of the rings obtained from the booty for making an ephod. There is no necessity, however, to understand this as signifying that 1700 shekels or 50 lbs. of gold had been used for the ephod itself, but simply that the making of the ephod was accomplished with this gold. The word <hi type="italic">ephod</hi> does not signify an image of Jehovah, or an idol, as <hi type="italic">Gesenius</hi> and others maintain, but the shoulder-dress of the high priest, no doubt including the <hi type="italic">choshen</hi> belonging to it, with the Urim and Thummim, as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.3">1Sa 14:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.10">1Sa 21:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.6">1Sa 23:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.9">1Sa 23:9</reference>, etc. The material for this was worked throughout with gold threads; and in addition to that there were precious stones set in gold braid upon the shoulder-pieces of the ephod and upon the choshen, and chains made of gold twist for fastening the choshen upon the ephod (see <reference osisRef="Exod.28.6-Exod.28.30">Ex 28:6-30</reference>). Now, if 50 lbs. of gold could not be used for these things, there were also fourteen precious stones to be procured, and the work itself to be paid for, so that 50 lbs. of gold might easily be devoted to the preparation of this state dress. The large quantity of gold, therefore, does not warrant us in introducing arbitrarily into the text the establishment of a formal sanctuary, and the preparation of a golden image of Jehovah in the form of a bull, as <hi type="italic">Bertheau</hi> has done, since there is no reference to פּסל or מסכה, as in Judg 17-18; and even the other words of the text do not point to the founding of a sanctuary and the setting up of an image of Jehovah.<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Oehler</hi> has correctly observed in <hi type="italic">Herzog's</hi> Cyclopaedia, that <hi type="italic">Bertheau</hi> acts very arbitrarily when he represents Gideon as setting up the image of a bull, as Jeroboam did afterwards, since there is nothing to sustain it in the account itself. Why cannot Gideon have worshipped without any image of Jehovah, with the help of the altar mentioned in Jdg 6:24, which was a symbol of Jehovah’s presence, and remained standing till the historian’s own time?</note> <div eID="gen3289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3290" type="x-p"/> The expression which follows, אתו ויּצּג, does not affirm that “heset it up<hi type="italic">,</hi>” but may also mean, “<hi type="italic">he kept it in his city of Ophrah</hi>.” הצּג is never used to denote the setting up of an image or statue, and signifies not only to put up, but also to lay down (e.g., Jdg 6:37), and to let a thing stand, or leave behind (<reference osisRef="Gen.33.15">Gen 33:15</reference>). The further remark of the historian, “<hi type="italic">and all Israel went thither a whoring after it, and it became a snare to Gideon and his house,</hi>” does not presuppose the founding of a sanctuary or temple in Ophrah, and the setting up of a golden calf there. In what the whoring of Israel after the ephod, i.e., the idolatry of the Israelites with Gideon’s ephod which was kept in Ophrah, consisted, cannot be gathered or determined from the use of the ephod in the worship of Jehovah under the Mosaic law. “The breastplate upon the coat, and the holy lot, were no doubt used in connection with idolatry” (<hi type="italic">Oehler</hi>), and Gideon had an ephod made in his town of Ophrah, that he might thereby obtain revelations from the Lord. We certainly are not for a moment to think of an exposure of the holy coat for the people to worship. It is far more probable that Gideon put on the ephod and wore it as a priest, when he wished to inquire and learn the will of the Lord. It is possible that he also sacrificed to the Lord upon the altar that was built at Ophrah (Jdg 6:24). The motive by which he was led to do this was certainly not merely ambition, as <hi type="italic">Bertheau</hi> supposes, impelling the man who, along with his followers, and maintained an independent attitude towards the tribe of Ephraim in the war itself (Jdg 8:1.), to act independently of the common sanctuary of the congregation which was within the territory of Ephraim, and also of the office of the high priest in the time of peace as well. For there is not the slightest trace to be found of such ambition as this in anything that he did during the conflict with the Midianites. The germs of Gideon’s error, which became a snare to him and to his house, lie unquestionably deeper than this, namely, in the fact that the high-priesthood had probably lost its worth in the eyes of the people on account of the worthlessness of its representatives, so that they no longer regarded the high priest as the sole or principal medium of divine revelation; and therefore Gideon, to whom the Lord had manifested himself directly, as He had not to any judge or leader of the people since the time of Joshua, might suppose that he was not acting in violation of the law, when he had an ephod made, and thus provided himself with a substratum or vehicle for inquiring the will of the Lord. His sin therefore consisted chiefly in his invading the prerogative of the <hi type="italic">Aaronic</hi> priesthood, drawing away the people from the one legitimate sanctuary, and thereby not only undermining the theocratic unity of Israel, but also giving an impetus to the relapse of the nation into the worship of Baal after his death. This sin became a snare to him and to his house. <div eID="gen3290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3291" type="x-p"/> The history of Gideon is concluded in Jdg 8:28-32. - Jdg 8:28. The Midianites had been so humiliated that they lifted up their head no more, and the land of Israel had rest forty years “<hi type="italic">in the days of Gideon,</hi>” i.e., as long as Gideon lived.
entries.ab09de6d01b1777cc806a73620dbbe1f61acece0: Jdg 8:29-31 <div eID="gen3291" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3292" type="x-p"/> Before the account of his death, a few other notices respecting his family are introduced for the purpose of preparing the way for the following history of the doings of his sons, in which the sin of Gideon came to a head, and the judgment burst upon his house. “<hi type="italic">And Jerubbaal, the son of Joash, went and dwelt in his house.</hi>” Both the word ויּלך, which simply serves to bring out the fact more vividly (see the remarks on <reference osisRef="Exod.2.1">Exo 2:1</reference>), and also the choice of the name <hi type="italic">Jerubbaal</hi>, merely serve to give greater prominence to the change, from the heat of the war against the Midianites to the quiet retirement of domestic life. Instead of accepting the crown that was offered him and remaining at the head of the nation, the celebrated Baal-fighter retired into private life again. In addition to the seventy sons of his many wives, there was a son born to him by a concubine, who lived at Shechem and is called his maid-servant in Jdg 9:18, and to this son he gave the name of <hi type="italic">Abimelech</hi>, i.e., king’s father. את־שׁמו ויּשׂם is not the same as את־שׁמו קרא, to give a person a name, but signifies to add a name, or give a surname (see <reference osisRef="Neh.9.7">Neh 9:7</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Dan.5.12">Dan 5:12</reference> in the Chaldee). It follows from this, that Abimelech received this name from Gideon as a cognomen answering to his character, and therefore not at the time of his birth, but when he grew up and manifested such qualities as led to the expectation that he would be a king’s father.
entries.97edc94791ee33048ed6fdd5999388b18170505a: Jdg 8:32 <div eID="gen3292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3293" type="x-p"/> Gideon died at a good old age (see <reference osisRef="Gen.15.15">Gen 15:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.25.8">Gen 25:8</reference>), and therefore also died a peaceful death (not so his sons; see Judg 9), and was buried in his father’s grave at Ophrah (Jdg 6:11). <div eID="gen3293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3294" type="x-p"/> Jdg 8:33-35 form the introduction to the history of Gideon’s sons.
entries.89a80c461daf9a534f0f7b754fa907e4bf98bc7b: Jdg 8:33 <div eID="gen3294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3295" type="x-p"/> After Gideon’s death the Israelites fell once more into the Baal-worship which Gideon had rooted out of his father’s city (Jdg 6:25.), and worshipped <hi type="italic">Baal-berith</hi> as their God. <hi type="italic">Baal-berith</hi>, the covenant Baal (equivalent to <hi type="italic">El-berith</hi>, the covenant god, Jdg 9:46), is not Baal as the god of covenants, but, according to <reference osisRef="Gen.14.13">Gen 14:13</reference>, Baal as a god in covenant, i.e., Baal with whom they had made a covenant, just as the Israelites had their faithful covenant God in Jehovah (see <hi type="italic">Movers</hi>, Phöniz. i. p. 171). The worship of Baal-berith, as performed at Shechem according to Jdg 9:46, was an imitation of the worship of Jehovah, an adulteration of that worship, in which Baal was put in the place of Jehovah (see <hi type="italic">Hengstenberg</hi>, Dissertations on the Pentateuch, vol. ii. p. 81).
entries.dc00113fc42fd4f97e1d7967d1d7947faed11876: Jdg 8:34-35 <div eID="gen3295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3296" type="x-p"/> In this relapse into the worship of Baal they not only forgot Jehovah, their Deliverer from all their foes, but also the benefits which they owed to Gideon, and showed no kindness to his house in return for all the good which he had shown to Israel. The expression <hi type="italic">Jerubbaal-Gideon</hi> is chosen by the historian here, not for the purely outward purpose of laying express emphasis upon the identity of Gideon and Jerubbaal (<hi type="italic">Bertheau</hi>), but to point to what Gideon, the Baal-fighter, had justly deserved from the people of Israel. Judgment upon the House of Gideon, or Abimelech’s Sins and End - Judges 9 <div eID="gen3296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3297" type="x-p"/> After the death of Gideon, Abimelech, his bastard son, opened a way for himself to reign as king over Israel, by murdering his brethren with the help of the Shechemites (Jdg 9:1-6). For this grievous wrong Jotham, the only one of Gideon’s seventy sons who escaped the massacre, reproached the citizens of Shechem in a parable, in which he threatened them with punishment from God (Jdg 9:7-21), which first of all fell upon Shechem within a very short time (vv. 22-49), and eventually reached Abimelech himself (Jdg 9:50-57).  <chapter eID="Judg.8"/> <div eID="gen3297" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:p n="21">21 Then Zeba and Zalmunna said, Rise thou and fall upon us: for as the man <ns0:hi>is,</ns0:hi> so <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> his strength <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Thou excellest him, as in Age and Stature, so in Strength; and it is more honourable, as well as easy, to die by the hands of a valiant man.</ns0:note>. And Gideon arose, and slew Zebah and Zalmunna, and took away the <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> orna<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ments like the moon.</ns0:note> ornaments that <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> on their camels necks.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22 ¶ Then the men of Israel said unto Gideon, Rule thou over us <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Not as a Judg, for he was already made by God; but as a King.</ns0:note>, both thou, and thy son, and thy sons son also <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Let the Kingdom be Hereditary to thee, and to thy Family.</ns0:note>: for thou hast delivered us from the hand of Midian <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">This miraculous and glorious deliverance by thy hands, deserves no less from us.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">23 And Gideon said unto them, I will not rule over you <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">To wit, as a King, which you desire.</ns0:note>, neither shall my son rule over you: the LORD shall rule over you <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">In a special manner, as he hath hitherto done, by Judges, whom God did particularly appoint and direct, even by <ns0:hi>Urim</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Thummim,</ns0:hi> and assist upon all occasions; whereas Kings had a greater Power, and onely a general dependence upon God, as other Kings had. Compare 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 8. 6, 7.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">24 ¶ And Gideon said unto them, I would desire a request of you, That ye would give me every man the ear-rings of his prey, (for they had golden ear-rings, because they were Ishmaelites <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Obj.</ns0:hi> They are called <ns0:hi>Midianites</ns0:hi> before. <ns0:hi>Ans.</ns0:hi> Here seems to have been a mixture of People, <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 6. 3. which are all called by one general name, <ns0:hi>Ishmaelites,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Arabi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ans,</ns0:hi> who used to wear Ear-rings, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 35. 4. but the great<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />est, and the ruling part of them were <ns0:hi>Midianites.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>.)</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="25">25 And they answered, We will willingly give <ns0:hi>them.</ns0:hi> And they spread a garment, and did cast therein, every man the ear-rings of his prey.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="26">26 And the weight of the golden ear-rings that he requested, <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> a thousand and seven hundred <ns0:hi>shekels</ns0:hi> of gold, beside ornaments, and <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> sweet Jewels.</ns0:note> collars, and purple raiment that <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> on the kings of Midian, and beside the chains that <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> about their camels necks.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="27">27 And Gideon made an ephod thereof <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Not of all of it; for then it would have been too hea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vy for use; but of part of it, the rest being probably em<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ployed about other things agreeable and appertaining to it; which elsewhere are comprehended under the name of the Ephod, as <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 17. 5. and 18. 14, 18. <ns0:hi>Hos.</ns0:hi> 3. 4.</ns0:note>, and put it in his city <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Not as a Monument of the Victory, for such Monuments were nei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther proper nor usual; but for Religious use, for which alone the Ephod was appointed. The cafe seems to be this, <ns0:hi>Gide<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on</ns0:hi> having by Gods Command erected an Altar in his own City, <ns0:hi>Ophrah, Iudg.</ns0:hi> 6. 26. for an extraordinory time and oc<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />casion, though it might be continued for ordinary use; and therefore as he intended to procure Priests, so he designed to make Priestly Garments, and especially an Ephod, which was the chief and most costly; which besides its use in sa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cred ministrations, was also the instrument by which the Mind of God was enquired and discovered, 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 26. 6, 9. and 30. 7. which might seem necessary for the Judg to have at hand, that he might consult with God upon all occasions.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>even</ns0:hi> in Ophrah: and all Israel went thither a whoring after it <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Committing Superstition or Idolatry with it, or going thither to enquire the Will of God; whereby they were drawn from the true Ephod, instituted by God for this end, which was to be worn by the High-Priest onely.</ns0:note>; which thing became a snare <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">An occasion of Sin and Ruine to him and his, as the next Chapter sheweth. Though <ns0:hi>Gideon</ns0:hi> was a good man, and did this with an honest mind, and a desire to set up Religion in his own City and Family; yet here seems to be many Sins in it; 1. Superstition and Will-worship, Worshipping God by a device of his own, which was fre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quently and expresly forbidden. 2. Presumption, in wear<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing, or causing other Priests to wear this kind of Ephod, which was peculiar to the High-Priest. 3. Transgression of a plain Command, of Worshipping God ordinarily but at one place and one Altar, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 12. 5, 11, 14. and with<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />drawing people from that place, to his. 4. Making a fear<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ful Schism or Division among the People. 5. Laying a Stumbling-Block, or an occasion of Superstition or Idola<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />try before that people, whom he knew to be too prone to it.</ns0:note> unto Gideon, and to his house.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="28">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:199" />28 ¶ Thus was Midian subdued before the chil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dren of Israel, so that they lifted up their head no more <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Recovered not their former Strength or Courage, so as to Conquer or Oppress others, as they had done.</ns0:note>: and the countrey was in quietness for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty years <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> To the fortieth year, from the beginning of the <ns0:hi>Midiani<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tish</ns0:hi> Oppression; see on <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 3. 11.</ns0:note> in the days of Gideon <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> As long as <ns0:hi>Gi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />deon</ns0:hi> lived.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="29">29 ¶ And Jerubbaal the son of Joash went and dwelt in his own house <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Not in his Fathers House, as he did before; nor yet in a Court like a King, as the People desired; but in a middle state, as a Judge, for the preservation and maintenance of their Religion and Liberties.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="30">30 And Gideon had threescore and ten sons <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> going out of his thigh.</ns0:note> of his body begotten: for he had many wives.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="31">31 And his concubine that <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> in Shechem <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">She dwelt there, and he oft came thither, either to execute Judgment, or upon other occasions.</ns0:note>, she also bare him a son, whose name he <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> called Abimelech <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">i. e. <ns0:hi>My Fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther the King;</ns0:hi> so he called him, probably, to gratify his Concubine, who desired it either out of Pride, or De<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sign.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="32">32 And Gideon the son of Joash died in a good old age <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">His long Life being Crowned with the continuance of his Honour, Tranquility and Happiness.</ns0:note>, and was buried in the sepulchre of Joash his father, in Ophrah of the Abi-ezrite.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="33">33 And it came to pass, as soon as Gideon was dead, that the children of Israel turned again <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Whereby we see the Wicked temper of this people, who did no longer cleave to God, than they were in a man<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ner constrained to it, by the Presence and Authority of their Judges.</ns0:note>, and went a whoring after Baalim <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">This was the general name including all their Idols, whereof one here follows.</ns0:note>, and made Baal-be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rith <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e. The Lord of the Covenant,</ns0:hi> so called, either from the Covenant wherewith the Worshippers of this God bound themselves to maintain his Worship, or to defend one another therein; or rather, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause he was reputed the God and Judg of all Covenants, and Promises, and Contracts, to whom it belonged to main<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tain them, and to punish the violaters of them; and such a God both the <ns0:hi>Grecians</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Romans</ns0:hi> had.</ns0:note> their god.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="34">34 And the children of Israel remembred not the LORD their God, who had delivered them out of the hand of all their enemies on every side:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="35">35 Neither shewed they kindness to the house of Jerubbaal, <ns0:hi>namely</ns0:hi> Gideon, according to all the goodness which he had shewed unto Israel.</ns0:p>
